findings.title: `?? []` / `|| 'fallback'` in toGenerated guard only nullish values, so a wrong-typed field is persisted and crashes every later read
findings.description: `RawBookResponse` is honest about optionality (schemas.ts:85-97 correctly marks every field `?`), but the coercions in `toGenerated` only defend against `null`/`undefined`. `data.keyInsights ?? []` passes a *string* straight through, and the assertion at line 52 means TypeScript never complains. The result is assigned to `Summary.keyInsights` which src/types.ts:59 declares as `string[]` — a lying type on a record that is written durably to IndexedDB by AddBookModal.tsx:78 and LibraryPage.tsx:93. Nothing re-validates on read. Every later consumer assumes the array: prompts.ts:36 `summary.keyInsights.join('\n')` (deep-dive generation), prompts.ts:67 and prompts.ts:70 (chat system instruction), prompts.ts:82 (audio script), plus `.map` in BookDetail. All throw `TypeError: ... .join is not a function` — so a single malformed generation permanently breaks chat, audio and deep-dive for that book. Same exposure on `actionableSteps` (line 37). Likelihood is lower than the missing-field cases because Gemini structured output usually honours ARRAY, but the cost is durable corruption and the guard is one `Array.isArray` per field. Correct behavior: validate with `Array.isArray(x) && x.every(i => typeof i === 'string')` before constructing the `Summary`, or run the parsed object through a guard function that returns `RawBookResponse | null`. Blast radius: both `summarizeBook` and `summarizePdf` funnel through `toGenerated`; 3 UI call sites persist its output.

findings.title: `response.text || '{}'` erases a blocked or truncated completion, fabricating a complete-looking Book that gets persisted
findings.description: The SDK types the accessor as `get text(): string | undefined` (genai.d.ts:5338). `undefined` is the real signal for a safety-blocked prompt, a `MAX_TOKENS` truncation, or an empty `candidates` array. `|| '{}'` coerces that signal away — and unlike a `!`, it fails silently instead of throwing. The empty object then flows through `toGenerated` (lines 22-41), where every field has a fallback: `data.title || fallbackTitle`, `data.category || 'Other'`, `data.rating ?? 0`, `data.readingTimeMinutes ?? 5`, `'No takeaway available.'`, `'No summary available.'`, `keyInsights: []`, `actionableSteps: []`. The function returns a structurally perfect `GeneratedBook` and its type promises a real generated summary. LibraryPage.tsx:90-94 then writes that straight to IndexedDB via `addBook`, and AddBookModal.tsx:69-79 does the same. The user asked for a summary, Gemini refused, and BookSum silently saves a book whose summary reads 'No summary available.' with an empty insights list — with no error surfaced anywhere (the catch on line 55 never fires). `'{}'` is also indistinguishable from the model legitimately returning `{}`. Correct behavior: treat `response.text === undefined` (or an empty/blocked `candidates[0]`) as an `AiError` of kind `'safety'` or `'malformed'` — `src/lib/ai/errors.ts:1-9` already has both kinds and user-facing copy for them (errors.ts:33,35), so nothing new needs designing. Same pattern at line 73 for the PDF path, quiz.ts:16 and recommend.ts:30. Blast radius: 4 parse sites; 2 UI entry points persist the result.

findings.title: generateDetailedSummary returns a failure sentinel typed as `string`, which callers persist as a real summary
findings.description: The declared return `Promise<string>` makes success and failure structurally identical — the caller cannot tell 'the model produced this markdown' from 'generation produced nothing'. `text` is empty whenever the stream yields no chunks: a safety block, an immediate `MAX_TOKENS` cut, or an empty candidate list (chunk.text is `string | undefined` per genai.d.ts:9465, and line 95 already coalesces it to ''). The sentinel is not just cosmetic — BookDetail.tsx:184-186 does `const longSummary = await generateDetailedSummary(...); const updated = { ...summary, detailedSummary: longSummary }; onSummaryUpdate(updated);`, persisting the literal string 'Failed to generate detailed summary.' into `Summary.detailedSummary` in IndexedDB. BookDetail.tsx:176 then short-circuits on `if (summary?.detailedSummary)` and opens the reader without regenerating, so from that point on the 'Read Full Summary' button permanently opens a reader displaying the failure message, with no UI path to retry. The catch on line 188 never fires because nothing threw. Correct shape: either throw an `AiError` (kind `'malformed'` or `'safety'` already exist in errors.ts:1-9) when `text` is empty, or return a tagged union (`{ ok: true; text: string } | { ok: false; reason: AiErrorKind }`) so the compiler forces the caller to handle the empty case before writing to storage. Blast radius: 1 call site (BookDetail.tsx:184), but the bad value is durable and self-perpetuating.

findings.title: base64 suite has two happy-path tests only; base64ToBytes is total in its type but throws on the one input path it serves
findings.description:
The whole suite is a round-trip of six clean bytes and one decode of a hand-written valid base64 string. Neither test feeds invalid base64, an empty string, a data-URL prefix, or a non-string coerced through `as`.

`base64.ts:5` declares `base64ToBytes(base64: string): Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>` — a total function with no error channel in its type. `atob` throws `InvalidCharacterError` (a `DOMException`) for any input containing characters outside the base64 alphabet. The function's ONLY production callers are `migrate.ts:136` and `migrate.ts:142`, which pass `legacy.pdfData` and `legacy.audioData` straight from `JSON.parse` of localStorage — values whose `string | undefined` type comes entirely from the `as T` assertion at `migrate.ts:58` and has never been validated. A legacy record holding `data:application/pdf;base64,JVBERi0...` (the natural way for the pre-IndexedDB app to have stashed a PDF) or a non-string throws here, and per L13-F03 that throw permanently hangs boot.

The migration test's own fixture at `migrate.test.ts:42` uses `btoa('fake pdf bytes')`, so it too can never reach this. Between the two suites, the decoder is proven only against input the tests themselves encoded. What goes untested: every real legacy `pdfData`/`audioData` value.

findings.title: base64ToBytes declares a total (string) => Uint8Array but atob throws on any non-base64 input, and it is fed unvalidated localStorage JSON
findings.description:
The signature `base64ToBytes(base64: string): Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>` claims a result for every `string`. It is a partial function: `atob` throws `DOMException: InvalidCharacterError` for any input containing a character outside the base64 alphabet, or whose length mod 4 === 1. Verified in a runtime harness: `atob('data:application/pdf;base64,JVBERi0x')` -> throws; `atob('not base64!!')` -> throws; `atob('AA=A')` -> throws; `atob('SGVsbG8')` (unpadded) -> succeeds. The declared return type carries none of this.

The input at the production call sites is unvalidated external data. `src/lib/storage/migrate.ts:54-62` does `JSON.parse(raw) as T` over a raw localStorage string, producing a `LegacyBook[]` whose `pdfData?: string` / `audioData?: string` fields are a compile-time fiction — localStorage is user- and extension-writable and the legacy app stored whole base64 PDFs there (the very thing CLAUDE.md records as what broke the original app). `migrate.ts:135-145` then calls `base64ToBytes(legacy.pdfData)` guarded only by a truthiness check.

There is no try/catch anywhere on the path. `migrateLegacyData` (migrate.ts:80) has none, and its only caller, `src/features/profile/ProfileContext.tsx:30-41`, invokes it as `void (async () => { await migrateLegacyData(); ... setIsLoading(false); })()` with no handler. Consequences of one malformed legacy blob: (1) the throw skips `setIsLoading(false)` at ProfileContext.tsx:41, so the app is stuck on its loading state permanently; (2) the throw happens before `localStorage.setItem(MIGRATION_MARKER, ...)` at migrate.ts:149, but AFTER `profiles.create()` (migrate.ts:90) and one or more `books.create()` have already committed — so on every subsequent reload the one-time migration re-runs from scratch and accumulates duplicate profiles, books and summaries. That is silent data corruption, and it is the declared-as-total return type that let the call site be written without a guard.

Correct behaviour: the boundary function should return `Uint8Array | null` (or throw a typed, documented error the caller is forced to handle), and the migration should validate/skip a malformed record rather than abort mid-loop.

Blast radius: `src/lib/storage/migrate.ts:136,142` (app-startup path for every user with legacy data) and `src/lib/ai/tts.ts:30`. Note that `bytesToBase64` (base64.ts:14) has no production caller at all — only `src/lib/base64.test.ts`.

findings.title: mockFetch types every API fixture as unknown, so no fixture is checked against the as-asserted response shapes
findings.description:
`mockFetch(handler: (url: string) => unknown)` returns `unknown`, so every response fixture in this file — `{ items: [{ volumeInfo: { imageLinks: { large } } }] }` on line 24, `{ docs: [{ cover_i: 12345 }] }` on line 36 — is invisible to the compiler. Those two assertions at `googleBooks.ts:12-14` and `openLibrary.ts:6` are the ONLY types the app has for two external HTTP APIs, and the tests that are supposed to pin them cannot detect drift between fixture and assertion in either direction.

Concrete gaps this creates:
- `googleBooks.ts:13` types `imageLinks?: Record<string, string>`. With `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` off (measured baseline), `links.extraLarge` is typed `string` — non-optional — while at runtime it is `undefined` for the vast majority of Google Books volumes, which return only `thumbnail`/`smallThumbnail`. The `??` chain on lines 19-23 works by accident of runtime `undefined`, not because the type says so. No fixture exercises an `imageLinks` object missing `large`, so the fallback ladder below line 20 is never executed by any test.
- No fixture produces a 200 with a non-JSON body, even though `mockFetch` can: a handler returning `undefined` makes `JSON.stringify(result)` evaluate to `undefined`, yielding a 200 with an empty body, and `response.json()` then throws `SyntaxError` — swallowed silently by the bare `catch {}` at `index.ts:17`, which would degrade every cover to a placeholder with no signal.
- No fixture exercises `items: [{}]` (an entry with no `volumeInfo`) or `docs: [{}]` (no `cover_i`).

What goes untested: the whole malformed/partial-response half of two `as`-asserted boundaries, plus the `Record<string, string>` claim that every key is a present string.

findings.title: Summary fixture always supplies real arrays, so the one consumer that would crash on an AI-shaped Summary is never exercised
findings.description:
The `summary` fixture is annotated `: Summary`, which is the right pattern and forces field completeness — but every array field is a hand-written real array (`keyInsights: ['Systems beat goals.', 'Identity drives habit.']`, `actionableSteps: ['Habit stack.']`), and the only variation the suite tries is the EMPTY array on line 70. Nothing in the lot ever hands `bookToMarkdown` a `Summary` whose fields came from `JSON.parse(...) as RawBookResponse`.

That matters because `markdown.ts` is the crash site for the untyped AI boundary. `summarize.ts:36` builds `keyInsights: data.keyInsights ?? []` from an unvalidated model response; `??` passes a string straight through. `markdown.ts:24-25` then does `if (summary.keyInsights.length > 0) { ...summary.keyInsights.map((i) => `- ${i}`) }` — a non-empty string satisfies `.length > 0` and then throws `TypeError: summary.keyInsights.map is not a function`, killing the library export. `markdown.ts:27-28` has the identical shape for `actionableSteps`.

So the type says `keyInsights: string[]`, the producer never checks, and the consumer's only tests supply values that make the claim true by construction. What goes untested: `bookToMarkdown`/`libraryToMarkdown` against any `Summary` that came off the wire rather than out of the test file. (The fixture itself is otherwise exemplary — explicitly annotated, complete, and the `Book` fixture on lines 5-18 likewise.)

findings.title: correctAnswerIndex is a bare number taken straight from unvalidated LLM JSON and persisted forever
findings.description:
`NewCardInput.correctAnswerIndex` is typed `number` and `newCard` copies it verbatim into a persisted `ReviewCard` (srs.ts:29) with no bounds check against `input.options`. The producer is `src/lib/ai/quiz.ts:16`, which does `JSON.parse(response.text || '{}') as { questions?: QuizQuestion[] }` — an unvalidated assertion over model output. The Gemini `responseSchema` at `src/lib/ai/schemas.ts:69-71` declares only `type: Type.NUMBER`; the range constraint lives in a `description` string ('Index (0-3) of the correct answer'), which is a prompt hint, not an enforced constraint. Structured output guarantees the JSON *type*, not the *range*.

Correct behaviour: `newCard` is the last gate before `reviewCards.upsert` writes to IndexedDB, so it must reject (or clamp) an index outside `0 <= i < options.length` and reject an `options` array that is empty. The type should express 'a valid index into options' — either a branded/refined index or a single `{ options, correctIndex }` value constructed through one validating factory — rather than two independent primitives.

Failure mode: a model that answers 1-indexed returns `correctAnswerIndex: 4` for a 4-option question. Nothing rejects it. The card is written to IndexedDB permanently. Thereafter `ReviewPage.tsx:94` (`showCorrect = isAnswered && index === current.correctAnswerIndex`) is false for every option, so no green 'correct' answer is ever shown, and `ReviewPage.tsx:76` (`isCorrect = selected === current.correctAnswerIndex`) is permanently false. The card stays in rotation forever and can never be answered correctly. No exception, no log, no way for the user to tell it is broken. Note the test suite already constructs exactly this impossible state and the types permit it: `src/features/review/reviewQueue.test.tsx:149-150` passes `options: []` with `correctAnswerIndex: 0`.

Blast radius: type declared at `src/lib/srs.ts:18` and `src/types.ts:89,108`; produced at `src/lib/ai/quiz.ts:16`; the sole persistence gate is `newCard` (`src/lib/srs.ts:22-36`), called from `src/components/QuizModal.tsx:53-60`; consumed at `src/features/review/ReviewPage.tsx:76,94` and `src/components/QuizModal.tsx:78,183`. Every generated quiz question in the app flows through this one line, and the damage is durable because it is written to IndexedDB.

findings.title: Migration test asserts summaryId but never the denormalised oneSentenceTakeaway it must move with
findings.description:
The `splits each legacy book into a Book and a Summary` test asserts `status`, `hasPdf`, `readingTimeMinutes` and `summaryId` on the migrated `Book`, and `keyInsights`/`model` on the `Summary`. It never asserts `atomic?.oneSentenceTakeaway` — even though the legacy fixture supplies it on line 33 (`oneSentenceTakeaway: 'Small changes compound.'`) and the migration reads it on `migrate.ts:125` to build the Summary.

`migrate.ts:105-119` builds the `Book` with `summaryId` set but WITHOUT `oneSentenceTakeaway`. `types.ts:41-50` documents `oneSentenceTakeaway` and `readingTimeMinutes` as deliberately denormalised onto `Book` so list views render without loading summaries, and `BookCard.tsx:89` reads exactly that field: `{book.oneSentenceTakeaway ? `"${book.oneSentenceTakeaway}"` : 'Not summarised yet'}`. So every migrated book renders "Not summarised yet" in the library grid despite having a full summary. The `AddBookModal.tsx:72` path sets it correctly, and `LibraryPage.tsx:92` re-syncs it after a generate — the migration is the one producer that drops it, and the one producer with no assertion covering it.

The type-system root cause: `Book.summaryId?` and `Book.oneSentenceTakeaway?` are two independently-optional fields that must be present or absent together. Nothing in the type makes `{ summaryId: set, oneSentenceTakeaway: undefined }` unrepresentable, so the compiler happily accepted the incomplete `books.create` call. A discriminated union on the summarised state (or a single required `summaryRef?: { id, takeaway }`) would have made this a compile error rather than a silent UI regression.

findings.title: LegacyProfile declares current-app union types for unvalidated JSON, and those values are persisted as a typed Profile
findings.description: The LegacyProfile interface at lines 38-44 annotates `favoriteVoice?: VoiceName` - the CURRENT app's five-member union - for data that is arbitrary JSON from localStorage. Nothing checks it. The value flows through profiles.create (repo.ts:22, where `??` only substitutes on null/undefined, never on a wrong type or an unknown string) and is persisted as `Profile.favoriteVoice: VoiceName`. From there it is read by src/features/book/BookDetailPage.tsx:43 and ReaderPage.tsx:26 and passed as the voice name to the Gemini TTS request, which will reject an unknown voice at request time - an AI failure with no diagnosable cause. src/components/ProfileView.tsx:281 also compares it against the known voice list, so the profile editor renders with no option selected. The same pattern applies to `monthlyGoal` (declared number, divided at ProfileView.tsx:53) and to `joinedAt` -> `createdAt`, which is the injection source for the boot-path crash described in L03-F02. Blast radius: one Profile per legacy user, but the profile is a singleton read by 26 profiles.* call sites and gates the entire app shell. Correct behaviour: narrow legacy fields with an explicit membership check against the union before persisting, and type the legacy shape with `string` (or unknown) rather than borrowing the current unions.

findings.title: Migration sets summaryId without the denormalised oneSentenceTakeaway, so every migrated book shows 'Not summarised yet'
findings.description: This is a real bug the type system should have caught. CLAUDE.md states oneSentenceTakeaway is deliberately denormalised onto Book so list views render without loading every summary. The normal creation path honours that (src/features/library/LibraryPage.tsx:92 spreads `{ ...book, oneSentenceTakeaway: summary.oneSentenceTakeaway }`), but the migration at lines 105-119 sets `summaryId` and then writes a full Summary at line 122-132 with `oneSentenceTakeaway: legacy.oneSentenceTakeaway ?? ''` while never backfilling the Book copy. Result: src/components/BookCard.tsx:89 renders `book.oneSentenceTakeaway ? ... : 'Not summarised yet'`, so every book imported from the legacy app displays 'Not summarised yet' in the library grid despite having a complete migrated summary. It compiles because types.ts declares `summaryId?: string` and `oneSentenceTakeaway?: string` as two independent optionals, so the impossible state 'summarised but no takeaway' is representable. A discriminated union - a summarised variant requiring both fields, an unsummarised variant permitting neither - would have made this a compile error, both here and at repo.ts:51-53 where the create input type inherits the same weakness. Blast radius: the bug hits every migrated book on the primary library screen; the type weakness covers all 22 books.* call sites.

findings.title: Legacy book fields are defaulted with ?? which guards nullish only, never type, then persisted as a typed Book
findings.description: Lines 106-118 use `??` as if it were validation. `??` substitutes only for null/undefined: any other value - a string where a number is declared, an unknown status string, an object - passes through untouched and is written by books.create as a `Book`. `legacy.status ?? 'Want to Read'` therefore persists `Book.status: BookStatus` holding e.g. 'Reading' or 'Currently Reading'; StatsView.tsx:15-16 buckets books by `b.status === 'Finished'` / `=== 'Want to Read'`, so such a book vanishes from both stat buckets and from the status filter while still counting in the library total. `legacy.rating ?? 0` and `legacy.readingTimeMinutes ?? 5` feed the arithmetic at StatsView.tsx:17-19 (see L03-F05) - a string there turns the reading-time total into concatenated digits. `legacy.priority` is passed with no default at all and is declared `Priority`. Blast radius: every migrated book, consumed by all 22 books.* call sites. Correct behaviour: a membership check for the union fields and a `typeof === 'number'` check for the numeric ones, falling back to the default when the check fails rather than only when the value is nullish.

findings.title: The only books.create fixture cannot produce a fat record, so the 'no binary data in records' invariant is unguarded
findings.description:
`bookInput()` is the sole fixture feeding `books.create` in the storage suite, and its `overrides` parameter is typed `Partial<Parameters<typeof books.create>[0]>` — which structurally forbids the fixture from ever carrying a key that isn't on `Book`. So no test in this file can produce the failure mode the repo is supposed to prevent.

`repo.ts:54-58` does `const book: Book = { ...input, id, addedAt }` and persists it verbatim. TypeScript's excess-property check does not fire on properties introduced by a spread, and does not fire at all when the argument is a variable rather than a fresh literal — which is exactly how `useLibrary.tsx:111` calls it during a library import: `await bookRepo.create({ ...book, profileId: profile.id })`, where `book` comes from `payload.books` of a `LibraryExport` produced by `JSON.parse(content) as LibraryExport` at `ProfileView.tsx:117`. That is an unvalidated user-supplied file. Any extra key on it — `pdfData`, `audioData`, a base64 cover — is copied straight into the `books` object store. CLAUDE.md names this as the exact defect that broke the original app ("No binary data in records... This is what broke the original app").

`migrate.test.ts:101` (`expect('pdfData' in (atomic as object)).toBe(false)`) is the only runtime guard for the invariant anywhere in the lot, and it covers the migration path only — not the import path, which is the one with an untrusted producer. What goes untested: `books.create` / `books.update` with any object carrying keys outside `Book`.

findings.title: profiles.list() types getAll output from the DBSchema declaration and immediately calls a string method on it
findings.description: `getAll('profiles')` is typed `Profile[]` purely because src/lib/storage/db.ts:8 declares `profiles: { key: string; value: Profile }`. That declaration is a promise about what is on disk, not a check of it - idb performs no validation. Line 9 then calls `a.createdAt.localeCompare(b.createdAt)` on every row. A record whose createdAt is not a string throws `TypeError: a.createdAt.localeCompare is not a function`. That is not hypothetical: migrate.ts:95 passes `legacyProfile?.joinedAt` (unvalidated JSON, see L03-F01) into profiles.create, where the `??` at repo.ts:24 only guards null/undefined - a numeric joinedAt is persisted verbatim as Profile.createdAt. profiles.list() is on the boot path (ProfileContext.tsx:32, awaited before setIsLoading(false) at line 40), so this throw hangs the app on its loading screen. Blast radius: 26 `profiles.*` call sites across src, and list() is the first storage read the app performs. Correct behaviour: validate rows at the repo boundary (a per-store guard that drops or repairs non-conforming records) rather than asserting the DBSchema shape and sorting on unchecked fields.

findings.title: books read path returns DBSchema-declared Book[] with no runtime guard; numeric fields are consumed in arithmetic downstream
findings.description: `getAllFromIndex('books', 'by-profile', profileId)` and `get('books', id)` are typed from db.ts:9, not verified. Every book in the app enters through these two lines, so any drift between the stored row and the current `Book` interface is invisible until a consumer misbehaves. Concrete failure: `Book.readingTimeMinutes` is declared `number` and src/components/StatsView.tsx:17 does `finished.reduce((acc, b) => acc + b.readingTimeMinutes, 0)`. If any row holds a string there (reachable via the legacy migration, migrate.ts:115, or the unvalidated backup import, L03-F04), `+` becomes string concatenation and the stats page renders a nonsense total like `045300` minutes with no error; if it holds undefined the total is NaN. Same class of exposure for `rating` (StatsView.tsx:19 divides by finished.length) and `addedAt` (LibraryPage.tsx:61 `new Date(b.addedAt).getTime()` yields NaN and the sort silently degrades). Blast radius: 22 `books.*` call sites; listByProfile is the source for every list view, stats view, export and search. Correct behaviour: a single validating read helper at this boundary, so the DBSchema declaration is checked once instead of trusted 22 times.

findings.title: books.create and summaries.upsert persist caller objects with no validation, and the backup-import path feeds them a user-picked file
findings.description: The repo is the mandated chokepoint for all writes (CLAUDE.md layering rule), but the write side performs zero runtime validation - it trusts the static parameter type and calls put(). That static type is a lie on the library-import path: src/components/ProfileView.tsx:117 does `JSON.parse(content) as LibraryExport` on a user-selected .json file, checks only `Array.isArray(data.books)` at line 119, and hands the whole payload to src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:110-116, which loops `bookRepo.create({ ...book, profileId })` and `summaryRepo.upsert(summary)` per element. Element shapes are never inspected. Two concrete failures: (a) a summaries element lacking `id` makes `put('summaries', ...)` reject with a DOMException DataError (keyPath 'id' yields no value, db.ts:30) mid-loop, after some books have already been written - a partial, non-atomic import; (b) a books element with a missing or wrong-typed field is persisted and thereafter claims to be a `Book` to every reader, corrupting the user's only copy of the library (local-first, no server backup). Note `payload.summaries ?? []` also only guards nullish - a non-array summaries field throws on for-of. Blast radius: 22 `books.*` and 6 `summaries.*` call sites all consume records this path can poison. Correct behaviour: validate at the repo's write boundary (the single place every writer must pass through) rather than trusting an assertion made three modules away.

findings.title: blobs.get trusts record.bytes and record.type verbatim; a non-ArrayBuffer silently produces a corrupt Blob instead of an error
findings.description: This is the ArrayBuffer/Blob conversion CLAUDE.md calls out as the boundary that broke the original app, and it performs no runtime check. `record.bytes` is typed ArrayBuffer only because types.ts:78 declares it so; `record.type` is an unconstrained string. The dangerous property of `new Blob([x])` is that it does not throw for a non-BlobPart - it stringifies. If bytes came back as `{}` (exactly what CLAUDE.md documents fake-indexeddb doing to a stored Blob, and what a partially-completed or hand-edited write produces), the result is a 15-byte Blob containing the text `[object Object]` carrying a legitimate `application/pdf` MIME type. src/components/BookDetail.tsx:197-200 then does `URL.createObjectURL(pdf)` and `window.open(url, '_blank')`, so the user gets a blank/broken PDF tab with no error anywhere - silent data loss presented as success. There is no `instanceof ArrayBuffer` check anywhere in src/lib/storage (verified by grep for typeof/Array.isArray/instanceof: zero hits in production storage code). Blast radius: 17 `blobs.*` call sites; blobs.get is the only read path for both PDF and generated audio. Correct behaviour: assert `record.bytes instanceof ArrayBuffer` at the boundary and reject/repair otherwise, so the failure is loud.

findings.title: Three independent Book fields encode the single fact "is this book summarised", and they disagree on how to spell "no"
findings.description: `readingTimeMinutes`, `oneSentenceTakeaway?` and `summaryId?` all encode one fact: whether a summary exists for this book. Three independently-mutable fields means 8 representable combinations where only 2 are valid, and the compiler cannot reject any of the 6 impossible ones. Worse, the three fields do not even agree on how absence is spelled: `oneSentenceTakeaway` and `summaryId` use `undefined`, but `readingTimeMinutes` is declared required and uses a magic `0` sentinel — `src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:157` writes `readingTimeMinutes: 0` for every Goodreads-imported book. The visible consequence is on one card: `src/components/BookCard.tsx:89` correctly narrows the optional and prints 'Not summarised yet', while `src/components/BookCard.tsx:95` on the very next line prints '0 min read' for that same unsummarised book, because a required `number` has no absent state to narrow. `src/components/StatsView.tsx:17` then sums those zeroes into the reading-time stat as if they were real measurements. Because there is no type-level link between the three fields, no write path is forced to keep them consistent: `useLibrary.tsx:82-83` (`if (book && book.summaryId !== summary.id) await bookRepo.update({ ...book, summaryId: summary.id })`) updates exactly one of the three when a book gains a summary and leaves the other two stale, and the compiler is satisfied. Correct shape: make `Book` a discriminated union — an unsummarised arm with none of the three fields, and a summarised arm where `summaryId: string`, `readingTimeMinutes: number` and `oneSentenceTakeaway: string` are all required together. Then 'summarised' becomes one narrowable fact instead of three, and a partial update stops compiling.

findings.title: LibraryExport declares a fully-formed backup shape but is only ever produced by an unchecked cast of a user-supplied file
findings.description: `LibraryExport` is the declared shape of a backup file the user picks off disk. The only place it is constructed from external data is `src/components/ProfileView.tsx:117`, which does `JSON.parse(content) as LibraryExport` with no validation beyond a shallow `Array.isArray(data.books)` check on line 119. Every `Book` and `Summary` inside is then trusted as fully-formed and written straight into IndexedDB by `src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:111` (`bookRepo.create({ ...book, profileId: profile.id })`). The type claims `books: Book[]` and `summaries: Summary[]` are non-optional and that each element has every required `Book` field; the runtime guarantees neither. The author evidently knew this: `useLibrary.tsx:109` and `:114` write `payload.books ?? []` and `payload.summaries ?? []` — nullish-coalescing fallbacks on two fields the type declares non-optional, which TypeScript considers unreachable dead code. That defensive `??` is the tell that the declared type and the real runtime shape have already diverged. Concrete failure: a hand-edited or truncated backup whose books lack `readingTimeMinutes` is written to the `books` store, then `src/components/StatsView.tsx:17` computes `finished.reduce((acc, b) => acc + b.readingTimeMinutes, 0)` and the whole total-reading-time stat becomes `NaN`, while `src/components/BookCard.tsx:95` renders the literal text `undefined min read`. The corruption is persistent — it survives reload because it went into IndexedDB. Correct behaviour: parse the file into `unknown` and run a real validator (a hand-written guard or a schema library) before anything reaches `bookRepo.create`, so `LibraryExport` is only ever obtained by proof rather than by assertion.

findings.title: QuizQuestion declares every field required but is populated by an unchecked cast of an LLM response
findings.description: `QuizQuestion` declares all four fields as required. Its only producer is `src/lib/ai/quiz.ts:16`: `const data = JSON.parse(response.text || '{}') as { questions?: QuizQuestion[] }` followed by `return data.questions ?? []` — raw Gemini output, asserted into the domain type with no per-element validation. A responseSchema is passed to the model (`src/lib/ai/schemas.ts:55-83`) but that is a generation hint, not an enforced contract, and it does not run on the client. The codebase already knows this rule and applied it correctly one file over: `src/lib/ai/schemas.ts:85-97` declares `RawBookResponse` with every field optional and the explicit comment 'Every field is optional because a model can always omit one, schema or not'. `QuizQuestion` is the same class of data and did not get the same treatment, so the two AI response types apply opposite discipline to identical risk. Concrete failure: the model omits `options` for one question, `data.questions` still passes the `?? []` guard, and `src/components/QuizModal.tsx:183` maps over `undefined` and throws a TypeError that takes down the quiz modal; if it instead omits `explanation`, the UI renders the string 'undefined' to the user. Correct behaviour: mirror `RawBookResponse` — declare a `RawQuizQuestion` with all fields optional, validate/normalise each element (drop malformed questions, backfill defaults) at the `quiz.ts` boundary, and only then hand out a `QuizQuestion` whose required fields are actually guaranteed.

findings.title: no-non-null-assertion is not enabled — 12 unguarded `!` assertions, and nothing stops more being added
findings.description:
`@typescript-eslint/no-non-null-assertion` is not part of `tseslint.configs.recommended` (it lives in the stylistic set) and the `rules` block in `eslint.config.js` does not add it. Confirmed via `--print-config`: the rule resolves to `-- NOT SET --`. The codebase currently carries 12 non-null assertions on 11 lines across 5 files: `src/components/ui/useFocusTrap.ts:47,48` (production — `items[0]!` and `items[items.length - 1]!`), plus 10 in tests (`src/lib/storage/migrate.test.ts` x4, `src/components/ui/toastStore.test.ts` x3, `src/features/review/reviewQueue.test.tsx` x2, `src/features/profile/ProfileContext.test.tsx` x1).

Each `!` is a claim the compiler is forbidden from checking and that crashes at runtime if wrong. The two production ones in `useFocusTrap.ts` sit on a focus-trap path where an empty `items` list is plausible (a dialog rendered before its children mount), and the test ones assert that repository reads returned a row — when that assumption breaks the test fails with an opaque `Cannot read properties of undefined` instead of a clear assertion message.

Correct behaviour: enable the rule (at minimum as `warn`) so the count cannot grow silently, and replace the existing sites with explicit guards or `toBeDefined()` assertions in tests. Adoption cost is trivial — 11 lines. This should land in the same change as L01-F02, because enabling `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` without this rule invites 10 new `!` as the path of least resistance.

findings.title: useRouteError() is unknown but is narrowed only by `instanceof Error`, so every 404 renders a generic message
findings.description:
`useRouteError()` is declared `(): unknown` (node_modules/react-router/dist/development/lib/hooks.d.ts:723). At runtime it yields one of two shapes: a thrown `Error`, or react-router's `ErrorResponse`. `ErrorResponseImpl` does NOT extend `Error` — it is a plain class (node_modules/react-router/dist/development/lib/router/utils.js:787 `var ErrorResponseImpl = class { status; statusText; data; ... }`). So `error instanceof Error` is definitively false for the whole `ErrorResponse` arm, and the component silently falls to the generic string.

CONCRETE FAILURE: navigate to any unmatched URL (mistyped path, stale bookmark, shared link with a typo). react-router builds `new ErrorResponseImpl(404, 'Not Found', new Error('No route matches URL "/typo"'), true)` (router.js:2742-2750). Because `routeTable` has exactly one top-level route, `getShortCircuitMatches` (router.js:2721 — `routes.length === 1 ? routes[0] : ...`) attaches that error to the root route, whose `errorElement` is this component (src/app/routes.tsx:16). The user therefore gets 'Something went wrong / An unexpected error occurred.' for a 404, and `status`, `statusText` and `data` are all discarded. Note the route table has no `path: '*'` catch-all, so this is the only 404 surface in the app.

react-router exports the discriminator for exactly this: `isRouteErrorResponse(error): error is ErrorResponse` (lib/router/utils.d.ts:958). It is not imported here. Adding it turns `unknown` into a real two-arm narrow and lets the boundary distinguish 'page not found' from 'the app crashed'.

VERIFIED NEGATIVE worth recording: there is NO `(error as Error).message` cast here. A thrown string, number, `null` or plain object falls to the fallback string rather than crashing the boundary. The `unknown` handling is safe, just incomplete.

BLAST RADIUS: every unmatched URL plus every `Response`/`ErrorResponse` thrown from anywhere in the route tree. `src/app/routing.test.tsx` covers `/`, `/book/:id`, `/stats` and back-navigation but never exercises the error path, so this is untested.

findings.title: routeTable is exported with no RouteObject[] annotation, which disables excess-property checking on the whole route tree
findings.description:
`export const routeTable = [...]` carries no type annotation. Because the array literal is bound to a variable before it reaches `createBrowserRouter` at line 31, its type loses object-literal freshness, and TypeScript's excess-property check never runs on it. A misspelled route key therefore compiles clean and silently produces a route that does nothing.

EMPIRICALLY VERIFIED with this repo's own compiler (node_modules/.bin/tsc, TypeScript 6.0.3) on an isolated probe reproducing react-router's `RouteObject = IndexRouteObject | NonIndexRouteObject` union (lib/router/utils.d.ts:535-562): the identical literal containing `errorELement` compiles with ZERO errors when the const is unannotated, and errors `TS2561: Object literal may only specify known properties, but 'errorELement' does not exist in type 'NonIndexR'. Did you mean to write 'errorElement'?` the moment the annotation is added. All `BaseRouteObject` members are optional, so nothing else catches the typo either.

WHY IT MATTERS HERE SPECIFICALLY: react-router pairs mutually-exclusive spellings that are easy to confuse — `element`/`Component`, `errorElement`/`ErrorBoundary`, `hydrateFallbackElement`/`HydrateFallback`. Writing `ErrorElement` or `Element` compiles today. If `errorElement` (line 16) were typo'd, the app would ship with no error boundary at all and `src/app/routing.test.tsx` would still pass — it covers `/`, `/book/:id`, `/stats` and back-navigation, never the error path.

NOTE ON CATEGORY: `routeTable` is an exported const, not a function. `untyped-public-function` is the closest enum member; the spec's Scope section explicitly lists 'exported value types' under missing/weak annotations. Re-bucket if the aggregate has a better home.

BLAST RADIUS: the entire route tree — six routes, the shell, and the error boundary. Fix shape is a one-word annotation: `export const routeTable: RouteObject[] = [...]`.

...

findings.title: handleAiError is typed total over `unknown` but throws on a null or undefined throwable
findings.description:
`handleAiError: (error: unknown) => string` is the contract three feature modules consume through `useShell()` (BookDetailPage.tsx:15, LibraryPage.tsx:19, ReaderPage.tsx:11) plus `AddBookModal` via its `onAiError` prop. The signature promises totality: hand it ANY value, get a string back. The implementation does not deliver that.

The `unknown` is accepted at the boundary and never narrowed anywhere along the chain. AppShell.tsx:48 forwards it verbatim to `toAiError`, which reads a property off it through `statusOf` (src/lib/ai/errors.ts:39-42): `const status = (error as { status?: unknown }).status;`. That assertion has no null guard, so `toAiError(null)` and `toAiError(undefined)` throw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'status')` rather than returning an `AiError`.

CONCRETE FAILURE: every call site is inside a `catch` block — LibraryPage.tsx:80, LibraryPage.tsx:98, AddBookModal.tsx:83. A throw from the error handler escapes the catch, propagates out of the render/event path, and unmounts the route into the root ErrorBoundary — which then (per L08-F02) renders 'An unexpected error occurred.' The failure handler becomes the crash.

REACHABILITY CAVEAT — stated honestly: nothing in `src/` throws a non-object (verified by grep for `throw null|undefined|'|"|{|<digit>` and bare `reject()` across src/ — zero hits), and `src/lib/ai/*` already wraps its throws in `toAiError`, so the common paths arrive as `AiError` and short-circuit at errors.ts:46. The trigger is a non-object rejection surfacing from `@google/genai` or `fetch`. Possible, not proven — hence medium, not high.

CORRECT SHAPE: narrow at the boundary. Either `statusOf` guards `typeof error === 'object' && error !== null` before the property read, or `handleAiError` narrows before forwarding. The permanent un-narrowed `unknown` is what lets the lie through.

BLAST RADIUS: four call sites, all in catch blocks, all on AI-feature paths.

findings.title: `reader.result as string` asserts away `ArrayBuffer | null` at the PDF file boundary, then indexes the split result without a bounds check
findings.description: `FileReader.result` is typed `string | ArrayBuffer | null`; the cast on line 42 tells the compiler it is always a string. It is a *type-safety* assertion over data the code did not produce (file contents), which is the boundary-erasure pattern: the assertion is currently true only because the caller happens to use `readAsDataURL` on line 46 — a detail four lines away that no type links to the cast. Change that call to `readAsArrayBuffer` and the code compiles unchanged while `.split` becomes a TypeError at runtime. Compounding it, `.split(',')[1]` is typed `string` (with `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` off) but is `string | undefined` at runtime, and the enclosing `Promise<string>` return type promises a string either way — a zero-byte or malformed selection can resolve `undefined` typed as `string`, which is then handed to `summarizePdf(base64)` and posted to Gemini as `inlineData`. Fix shape: narrow instead of assert — `typeof reader.result === 'string' ? ... : reject(...)` — and check the comma split before resolving. Blast radius: the AddBookModal PDF path only, but it is the app's one arbitrary-file ingress.

findings.title: A file is accepted as "a PDF" on the strength of the browser-reported `File.type` alone, and the advertised 10MB limit is never enforced
findings.description: The only validation applied to a user-chosen file is `selected.type === 'application/pdf'` (line 91). `File.type` is not content-sniffed — on Windows it is derived from the extension via the registry, so any file renamed to `.pdf` reports `application/pdf`. After that single check, `file` lives in state typed `File | null` and every downstream type asserts PDF-ness without re-checking: it is base64'd (line 64), sent to Gemini as PDF `inlineData` via `summarizePdf`, and persisted as `blobs.put(book.id, 'pdf', options.pdf)` with `StoredBlob.kind: 'pdf'` (types.ts:69-71) — a type that claims the bytes are a PDF when nothing ever verified it. Separately, the UI advertises "Maximum size: 10MB" (line 250) and no code anywhere enforces it: `handleFileChange` checks only the MIME string, and `handleSubmit` has no size guard. A 500MB file is accepted, read fully into a data URL (~1.37x in memory), and posted — the tab OOMs or the request is rejected far downstream with an opaque AI error. Fix shape: validate at the boundary — check `selected.size` against the advertised limit and sniff the `%PDF-` magic bytes (or at minimum the extension AND type) before the file is allowed into state; consider a `ValidatedPdf` wrapper type so downstream code cannot receive an unchecked `File`. Note the sibling ingress (Goodreads CSV) is audited elsewhere; this is the add-a-book path.

findings.title: BookDetail reads the Summary's takeaway while BookCard reads the denormalised copy, and they visibly disagree
findings.description: The same fact is stored twice with different types and no invariant tying them: `Summary.oneSentenceTakeaway` is required `string` (types.ts:57) and `Book.oneSentenceTakeaway` is optional `string` (types.ts:48). BookDetail line 452 renders the Summary copy; `BookCard.tsx:89` renders the Book copy with a falsy fallback (`book.oneSentenceTakeaway ? ... : 'Not summarised yet'`). Nothing keeps them in sync: `book.oneSentenceTakeaway` is written ONLY at creation time (`AddBookModal.tsx:72`, `LibraryPage.tsx:92`), and `saveSummary` (useLibrary.tsx:78-88) syncs only `book.summaryId` back onto the book - never the takeaway. WHAT THE USER SEES: a book whose stored `oneSentenceTakeaway` is `''` (migrate.ts:125 writes exactly that for legacy records, and any imported backup can carry it) has a real Summary with `summaryId` set, yet its BookCard says 'Not summarised yet' in the library while opening it shows the genuine takeaway quoted in the orange panel - the library and the detail view contradict each other about the same book. The optional-vs-required typing is what permits it: the compiler cannot express 'if `summaryId` is set then `oneSentenceTakeaway` is a non-empty string'. FIX SHAPE: fold the denormalised fields into the tagged union proposed in L11-F02 so they can only be absent together, and have `saveSummary` write the takeaway back onto the Book whenever the Summary changes. Note the denormalisation itself is deliberate (CLAUDE.md) and should be kept - only the sync and the typing need fixing.

findings.title: `e.target?.result as string` erases three real possibilities from FileReader's result
findings.description: `ProgressEvent.target` is `EventTarget | null` and `FileReader.result` is `string | ArrayBuffer | null`, so the expression's honest type is `string | ArrayBuffer | null | undefined`. The `as string` tells the compiler all four cases are one. On the happy path `readAsText` does produce a string, but on an aborted or failed read `result` is `null`, and `JSON.parse(null)` coerces to the string `'null'` and returns `null` - so `data` is `null`, line 119's `data.books` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null`, and the user gets the generic 'Could not read that backup file.' message with no indication the read itself failed. The assertion is currently masked by the surrounding catch rather than being correct, and it is the same cast that feeds the unvalidated write in L11-F04. FIX SHAPE: narrow instead of assert - `const result = e.target?.result; if (typeof result !== 'string') { toast.error(...); return; }` - which costs two lines and removes both the lie and the misleading error message.

findings.title: `Book.rating: number` conflates "unrated" with "rated 0", so the average-rating stat is silently wrong for imported libraries
findings.description: `Book.rating` is a required `number` (types.ts:36) with no representation for "not rated". The Goodreads importer therefore substitutes a sentinel: `rating: Number.isFinite(rating) ? rating : 0` (goodreads.ts:111). StatsView then averages every Finished book's rating unconditionally (line 20), so each unrated import drags the mean toward zero — a user who imports 200 Goodreads books and rated 10 of them sees "Avg. Rating 0.2" presented as a fact about their taste. The type system cannot catch it because `0` is a perfectly good `number`. BookCard has the mirrored symptom, rendering `{book.rating}/5` for every Finished book (BookCard.tsx:100), so unrated imports display an authoritative-looking "0/5". Secondary weakness on the same lines: the ternary makes `avgRating` an accidental `string | number` union (`.toFixed(1)` returns `string`, the empty-library branch returns the number `0`), which is why `StatCard.value` had to be widened to `string | number` (line 197) — the display type now accepts anything numeric-or-textual and no longer documents what a stat card shows. Fix shape: make the domain explicit — `rating?: number` (or a branded `Rating` 1..5 with an explicit unrated state) so `reduce` cannot silently include sentinels, and return a single formatted `string` from the memo. Blast radius: StatsView's headline stat plus every BookCard rating badge.

findings.title: Pending-confirm state is split across a nullable state field and a nullable ref that the types never tie together, so `Promise<boolean>` can hang forever
findings.description: A pending confirmation is one logical thing represented as two independent nullable slots: `options: ConfirmOptions | null` (line 18) and `resolverRef: ((value: boolean) => void) | null` (line 19). The invariant `options !== null` <=> `resolverRef.current !== null` is real but unencoded, and the code violates it: `confirm()` assigns `resolverRef.current = resolve` unconditionally (line 24), so a second `confirm()` issued while one is pending overwrites the first resolver with no trace. The first promise then never settles. The declared contract `type ConfirmFn = (options: ConfirmOptions) => Promise<boolean>` (line 13) claims every call yields a settling promise; the runtime does not deliver that. Concrete failure: a consumer does `if (!(await confirm({...}))) return;` before a destructive action (all three consumers do — ProfilePage.tsx:10, BookDetailPage.tsx:16, ProfileView.tsx:49). If a second confirm is raised — a double-click on a delete control, or a second component racing on the same provider — the first `await` never resumes, so its `finally`/spinner-reset never runs and its enclosing async function is retained forever. The same shape means unmounting the provider mid-confirm leaks a pending promise. The `?? ''` and `?.` fallbacks scattered through the JSX (lines 41, 45, 51, 56, 61) exist purely because the type cannot express "open implies options". Fix shape: one state value shaped as a discriminated union — `{ status: 'idle' } | { status: 'pending'; options: ConfirmOptions; resolve: (v: boolean) => void }` — and have `confirm()` settle any existing pending entry with `false` before replacing it. Blast radius: 3 consumers, all on destructive paths (delete profile, delete book).

findings.title: `querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>` is an unchecked assertion over a runtime selector string in the app's shared focus trap
findings.description: `querySelectorAll<E extends Element>(selectors: string): NodeListOf<E>` does not validate `E` against the selector — supplying `HTMLElement` is an assertion, indistinguishable in safety from `as HTMLElement[]`, over a selector string the compiler never parses. Two of the six clauses in `FOCUSABLE` (line 5) — `a[href]` and `[tabindex]:not([tabindex="-1"])` — match non-HTML elements: an `<a>` inside inline SVG is an `SVGAElement`, and any SVG node carrying `tabindex` matches too. The codebase renders inline SVG in every dialog (lucide-react icons inside the close buttons of Dialog.tsx:46, QuizModal.tsx:171, ChatModal.tsx:120, DailyWisdomModal.tsx:44), so the selector runs against SVG content on every open. The assertion also claims nothing about *visibility*: `display:none`/`visibility:hidden`/`inert` controls match the selector, so `focusable()[0]?.focus()` (line 26) can be a silent no-op on a hidden first control, and the Tab wrap-around at lines 51-57 then compares `document.activeElement` against elements that can never hold focus — the trap stops wrapping and Tab escapes the modal to the page behind it, which is the accessibility guarantee the hook exists to provide. Fix shape: keep the query as `Element`, then narrow with a real guard (`instanceof HTMLElement` plus an offsetParent/`checkVisibility()` filter) so the array type is earned rather than asserted. Blast radius: this is the single shared trap for every modal surface in the app — Dialog (used by AddBookModal.tsx:100, ApiKeyDialog.tsx:38 and ConfirmDialog.tsx:39), plus ChatModal.tsx:34, QuizModal.tsx:31 and DailyWisdomModal.tsx:22 which call it directly. Related: the hook's `{ active: boolean }` parameter encodes no notion of a trap *stack*, and both effects register on `document`, so two simultaneously-active traps both handle the same Escape/Tab (line 38's `stopPropagation` does not stop sibling listeners on the same node — that would need `stopImmediatePropagation`). CLAUDE.md documents "never leave two `aria-modal` dialogs open at once" as a convention; the types provide no enforcement of it.

findings.title: Optional chain over Array.find's Book | undefined makes the summaryId assertion vacuous
findings.description: `imported.find(...)` (line 53) returns `Book | undefined`, and the test then narrows with `?.` rather than proving the book exists. Line 55, `expect(atomic?.summaryId).toBeUndefined()`, PASSES when `atomic` itself is undefined -- i.e. if the Atomic Habits row were never imported at all, the assertion that it has no summary would still be green. This is the mirror-image of a non-null assertion: instead of lying that a value exists, the optional chain silently converts a type-level `| undefined` into a passing test. The only reason the suite still catches a missing book is the incidental `toHaveLength(2)` at line 51 and the fact that lines 56 and 60 use matchers that throw on undefined. Fix shape: `expect(atomic).toBeDefined()` first, then assert on a narrowed value, so the 'row not imported' failure mode reports as a failure rather than as a pass. Same optional-chain-over-index pattern in reviewQueue.test.tsx:93-96 and 110-111, where `const [stored] = ...` is then mixed inconsistently as `stored?.id` and `stored!.dueAt` on adjacent lines.

findings.title: The 200-book scale test hand-builds rows and bypasses parseGoodreadsCsv, the only validation in the feature
findings.description: The 'imports a large library without any AI cost' test constructs 200 objects `{ title, author, status: 'Want to Read' as const, rating: 0 }` and passes them straight to api.importGoodreadsRows. They satisfy GoodreadsRow structurally only because isbn13 and dateRead are optional (goodreads.ts:8-9), so the fixture never crosses the parser -- the single place in the feature where junk could be rejected. The result is that the parser -> importer seam is only ever exercised with the 2 well-formed rows of the CSV literal, while the only scale coverage runs on pre-sanitised data. Two consequences go untested: (a) the ISBN branch, since all 200 rows omit isbn13 so `coverForIsbn(undefined)` (goodreads.ts:121-122) returns undefined and every book falls to `placeholderCover(title)` -- the openlibrary cover URL path is covered by exactly one row; (b) the dedupe key `title.trim().toLowerCase()|author.trim().toLowerCase()` (useLibrary.tsx:132-133), which is trivially satisfied by 200 distinct titles all authored 'Someone' -- no test covers rows whose titles differ only by case, whitespace or a trailing series suffix, which is the realistic duplicate shape in a real export. importGoodreadsRows also declares no validation of its own on the GoodreadsRow[] it accepts.

findings.title: Import workflow held as three independent states, letting a failed pick import the previous file's rows
findings.description: `preview`, `filename` and `isImporting` model one linear workflow as three orthogonal states -- eight representable combinations for four legal ones (`filename` set with `preview` null, and vice versa, are both representable and both meaningless). The illegal combination is reachable: `handleFile`'s catch on line 30 toasts and returns without clearing `preview` or `filename`, because both are only assigned on the success path (lines 25-26). Concrete failure: the user picks A.csv successfully (preview shows '100 books found', the drop zone shows 'A.csv'), then re-opens the picker and chooses B.csv, whose read rejects -- `file.text()` throws `DOMException: NotReadableError` / `NotFoundError` when the file was moved, deleted, or its permission revoked between selection and read, and on a disconnected network share. The user sees 'Could not read that file.' but the drop zone still reads 'A.csv', the preview still reads '100 books found', and the Import button is still enabled; clicking it imports A's rows while the user believes they are importing B. Correct shape: a single tagged state, `{ phase: 'idle' } | { phase: 'parsed'; filename: string; result: GoodreadsParseResult } | { phase: 'importing'; ... }`, which makes the stale combination unrepresentable and forces the error path to transition explicitly. Blast radius: this component only, but the outcome is persisted book records.

findings.title: localStorage recommendation cache is cast to a concrete shape and rendered without validation
findings.description: `JSON.parse(cached) as { at: number; items: Recommendation[] }` is a pure assertion over external, persistent, user-writable storage. The value flows unchecked into `setRecommendations(parsed.items)` and then into RecommendationCarousel.tsx:79 `recommendations.map(...)` and `rec.title` / `rec.author` / `rec.description` / `rec.coverUrl`. The try/catch on line 39 only covers `JSON.parse`, i.e. syntax errors -- a syntactically valid but wrong-shaped value passes the assertion, and the resulting failure happens later during the carousel's render, outside the catch, so the self-healing `localStorage.removeItem` on line 40 never runs. Concrete failure: a stored `{"at":,"items":"abc"}` satisfies the `parsed.items?.length` truthiness test (string length 3) and then throws `TypeError: recommendations.map is not a function` from the error boundary -- on every load, permanently, because the poison stays in localStorage. Milder always-live version: entries missing `coverUrl` render `` (React drops the attribute, so `onError` and the placeholder fallback on line 94 may never fire) and entries missing `title` produce `key={undefined}`. Reachability: the app is the only writer today, but a shared origin makes localStorage non-exclusive -- the planned Phase 4 GitHub Pages demo puts BookSum on `.github.io`, one origin shared with every other Pages site under that account -- and any future change to `Recommendation` leaves 24h of stale-shaped caches that still pass the TTL check. Correct behaviour: validate the parsed object (array check plus per-item field check) and drop the cache when it fails, the way ProfileView.tsx:119 at least array-checks its import.

findings.title: LibraryPage renders the zero-books empty state during the initial load because it never reads `isLoading`
findings.description: Consumer-side manifestation of L09-F03, on the app's default route. Line 18 destructures only `{ books, addBook, getSummary }` -- `isLoading` is available on the same object and is simply not taken -- so `filteredBooks.length > 0 ? grid : emptyState` treats the loading `[]` as 'this user has no books'. App.tsx:12 gates on `useProfile().isLoading`, not on the library's, so `LibraryProvider` mounts with a settled profile while `books` is still `[]` and `isLoading` is still `true`. The first paint of `/` for a user with 500 imported books is therefore 'Your library is quiet' plus an 'Add Your First Book' button, for the duration of the IndexedDB open + index read. The same array also drives `categories` (line 65), so the topic filter row is empty in that window. This is only possible because the producer's type does not tag its states; the fix here is to consume the tag (render a skeleton while loading), and it disappears entirely once L09-F03 is fixed. Blast radius: the default route, every cold load.

findings.title: The feature's entire public contract is inferred: `LibraryApi = ReturnType<typeof useLibraryState>`
findings.description: `useLibraryState` is module-private and carries no return type annotation; `LibraryApi` is derived from it with `ReturnType<>`, and `useLibrary(): LibraryApi` therefore has an annotation that is just an alias for 'whatever the implementation currently happens to return'. Nothing declares what this module promises. An incidental change inside any of the ten `useCallback`s -- a widened parameter, a narrowed return, a renamed key in the returned object literal -- silently rewrites the feature's public API, and TypeScript reports the breakage at the six consumer sites rather than at the source. There is no interface to diff a PR against and no place to document the contract. The repo already has the idiomatic fix one folder over: src/features/profile/ProfileContext.tsx:9-18 declares `interface ProfileContextValue` explicitly and annotates `useProfile(): ProfileContextValue`. `LibraryProvider` (line 193) likewise has no return annotation. Blast radius: six app call sites (AppShell.tsx:27, LibraryPage.tsx:18, StatsPage.tsx:6, ProfilePage.tsx:9, BookDetailPage.tsx:13, useBookRoute.ts:10, GoodreadsImport.tsx:13) plus two test files that re-derive `ReturnType<typeof useLibrary>`.

findings.title: selectProfile is wired behind a non-null assertion that would throw, and no test ever clicks it
findings.description: The probe wires `selectProfile(allProfiles[0]!.id)` behind a non-null assertion. That assertion is false in two of the file's own tests -- 'starts with no active profile' (lines 36-39) and 'ignores a stale persisted id' (lines 74-78) both leave allProfiles empty -- so the button would throw a TypeError if clicked. No test clicks it, which means selectProfile (ProfileContext.tsx:49-54) is exercised by zero tests, including its `if (!found) return` branch: selecting a profile that was deleted in another tab is a silent no-op with no UI feedback and no toast. Worse, `updateProfile` and `deleteProfile` -- 2 of the 8 members of ProfileContextValue (ProfileContext.tsx:9-18) -- are not even destructured by the probe (line 9), so deleteProfile's localStorage.removeItem side effect buried inside a setProfile state updater (ProfileContext.tsx:73-77), which React StrictMode double-invokes, is entirely untested. UNTESTED PRODUCTION BEHAVIOUR: profile switching, profile renaming/goal editing, and profile deletion including its cascade through repo.ts:36-38.

findings.title: ProfileContextValue models loading and profile as independent fields, so the type permits acting on a null profile mid-load
findings.description:
`ProfileContextValue` exposes `profile: Profile | null` and `isLoading: boolean` as orthogonal fields. The three states that actually exist — loading (profile not yet known), settled-with-profile, settled-without-profile — are encoded as four representable combinations, and the compiler cannot tell them apart. `profile === null` is ambiguous between 'still loading' and 'no profile selected', which is exactly the failure CLAUDE.md records as learned the hard way: 'Hooks that depend on the profile must wait for useProfile().isLoading to settle, or they will act on a null profile and silently drop the write.' The type does not enforce that rule; it is documentation only, which is why `useLibrary.tsx:25` and `useReviewQueue.ts:14` each hand-roll the same `if (profileLoading) return;` line with a comment explaining why.

Blast radius: 10 non-test consumers of `useProfile()`. Only 3 read `isLoading` (`App.tsx:10`, `useLibrary.tsx:18`, `useReviewQueue.ts:9`). The other 7 — `useTheme.ts:15`, `AppShell.tsx:26`, `ProfilePage.tsx:8`, `ProfilePicker.tsx:7`, `LibraryPage.tsx:17`, `BookDetailPage.tsx:14`, `ReaderPage.tsx:10` — destructure `profile` and treat `null` as 'no profile', with the type raising no objection.

Honest scoping: there is no live bug, because `App.tsx:12-18` gates the entire tree on `isLoading` before rendering anything, so no consumer in this lot can observe the loading state. That single gate is the only thing making the other 7 consumers correct, and it is invisible to the type system. Move it, add a route outside it, or render any of these components in a test/Storybook harness without the gate, and the silent-drop class returns with no compiler error — e.g. `useTheme.setTheme` (useTheme.ts:33-39) returns `Promise<void>` that resolves as if the write succeeded while `if (!profile) return;` discards it.

Correct behavior: a tagged union (`{ status: 'loading' } | { status: 'ready'; profile: Profile } | { status: 'no-profile' }`) so `profile` is only reachable after narrowing, making the gate compiler-enforced instead of convention-enforced. Verified negatives in this file: `createContext<ProfileContextValue | undefined>(undefined)` (line 20) is honest — no `null as unknown as T` default — and `useProfile()` throws outside the provider (line 113) and annotates its return explicitly.

findings.title: correctAnswerIndex is never bounds-checked against options.length, so a card can be silently impossible to answer correctly
findings.description:
`ReviewCard.correctAnswerIndex` is a bare `number` (src/types.ts:89) with no bound relating it to `options.length`, and it arrives from the same unvalidated path as F01 (model JSON cast at `quiz.ts:16`, persisted by `QuizModal.tsx:58`, re-typed from IndexedDB by `repo.reviewCards.listDue`). The schema's '0-3' constraint is a prose `description` (src/lib/ai/schemas.ts:71), not an enforced range. Nothing in `useReviewQueue` or `ReviewPage` checks `0 <= correctAnswerIndex < options.length`.

Worth being precise about the failure mode: `ReviewPage` never does `options[correctAnswerIndex]`, so there is no `undefined` render and no crash. It compares indices (lines 76 and 94). With an out-of-range index (say 7 against 4 options, or a negative), `showCorrect` is false for every rendered option and `isCorrect` is false for every possible selection. The user answers, no option is highlighted green, whatever they picked is highlighted red, and the explanation claims a correct answer that is not on screen. The card is permanently un-answerable-correctly and stays in rotation being marked wrong forever. Because the user can still grade it, this degrades quietly rather than blocking — which is why it is likely to go unnoticed and unreported.

Correct behavior: validate the index against the options array at the boundary where cards enter typed code, and model the pair as a single validated unit rather than two independent primitives. Blast radius: every card produced by quiz generation; the identical unguarded comparison also exists in `QuizModal.tsx:78` and `:183`, so the same malformed data misbehaves in the in-quiz flow too.

findings.title: The probe binds to an inferred hook contract in which current: queue[0] is typed ReviewCard, not ReviewCard | undefined
findings.description: `let api: ReturnType<typeof useReviewQueue>` inherits whatever the hook infers, and useReviewQueue (useReviewQueue.ts:8) declares no return type. Its `current: queue[0]` (useReviewQueue.ts:46) therefore infers as `ReviewCard`, not `ReviewCard | undefined`, because noUncheckedIndexedAccess is off -- the hook's public contract states that a card always exists, which is false the moment the queue empties (which is the normal end of every session, and the state asserted at lines 65 and 91). The test itself proves the type is wrong: lines 56, 77 and 128 all write `api.current?.question` with an optional chain the compiler considers unnecessary. A consumer that trusts the declared type and writes `current.question` compiles and crashes on the empty queue; ReviewPage.tsx:52 happens to guard with `if (!current)` but nothing in the type system requires that and no test would catch a consumer that omits it. The same untyped-return pattern applies to useLibraryState (useLibrary.tsx:17, re-exported as LibraryApi at line 185) and useTheme (useTheme.ts:14). Fix shape: annotate the hook's return with an explicit interface declaring `current: ReviewCard | undefined`.

findings.title: useReviewQueue has no return annotation, so `current` is inferred as a definite ReviewCard while the runtime returns undefined
findings.description:
`useReviewQueue` is exported with no explicit return type, so its contract is whatever TypeScript infers from the returned object literal. With `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` off (tsconfig.json sets only `strict: true`), `queue[0]` infers as `ReviewCard`, not `ReviewCard | undefined`. The hook's public type therefore states that `current` is always a card — which is false for the overwhelmingly common case of an empty queue (nothing due), and false on first paint before `reload()` resolves.

No crash today: `ReviewPage.tsx:52` guards with `if (!current)` and renders the 'Nothing due' state, and `useReviewQueue.ts:36-37` guards internally with `const [current] = queue; if (!current) return;`. Both guards are correct — and both are, as far as the compiler is concerned, dead code testing a value that can never be falsy. That is the actual danger: the type actively argues against the only thing keeping the feature alive. A second consumer (a nav badge doing `current.question.slice(0, 40)`, a keyboard-shortcut handler, a test helper) gets zero compiler pressure to guard and throws `Cannot read properties of undefined`. Equally, enabling `@typescript-eslint/no-unnecessary-condition` — not currently configured in eslint.config.js, which runs untyped rules only — would report both existing guards as removable, inviting a 'cleanup' that turns the empty-queue path into a hard crash on the Review page.

Correct behavior: annotate the hook's return with `current: ReviewCard | undefined` (or enable `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`) so the guard is required rather than tolerated. Blast radius: currently one consumer (`ReviewPage`), so this is refactor-safety rather than a live defect; the fix is trivial and makes both existing guards provably load-bearing.

findings.title: vi.stubGlobal erases the matchMedia type, and the hand-built stub never fires a change event
findings.description: mockPrefersDark installs a hand-built matchMedia through vi.stubGlobal, whose value parameter is typed `unknown` -- TypeScript performs NO check that the stub satisfies `(query: string) => MediaQueryList`. The stub's `addEventListener: vi.fn()` records calls and never invokes the handler, so useTheme.ts:22-24 -- `const onChange = (event: MediaQueryListEvent) => setSystemDark(event.matches)` and the removeEventListener cleanup -- is dead code from this suite's point of view. Both 'system' tests (lines 61-71) set the preference BEFORE mount and assert the initial resolution from useState(systemPrefersDark) (useTheme.ts:17); nothing ever flips the preference while mounted. Compounding it, useTheme.ts:23-24 uses an optional call (`query.addEventListener?.(...)`), so if the stub -- or a real browser -- ever lacks that method the hook silently stops subscribing and every test still passes green. UNTESTED PRODUCTION BEHAVIOUR: a user on `theme: 'system'` who switches their OS between light and dark with the app open; the app should re-theme live and there is no test that it does.

findings.title: sendMessageStream returns `Promise<string>` that is silently empty on a blocked completion, leaving a permanently blank chat bubble
findings.description: `chunk.text` is `string | undefined` in the SDK (genai.d.ts:9465) and line 33 coalesces it to `''`. If the model produces no text at all — a safety block on the reply, an immediately-truncated stream, or an empty candidate list — the loop completes without throwing and the function returns `''`. The return type `Promise<string>` cannot express that difference, so callers have no compiler-visible reason to handle it. ChatModal.tsx:59 pushes a placeholder `{ role: 'model', text: '' }` before the call, `onChunk` is never invoked so the placeholder is never filled, and the recovery code at ChatModal.tsx:70-79 lives in a `catch` that never fires. The user sees an empty assistant bubble that stays empty, with no error toast and no retry affordance. The catch block is even written to replace a model message whose `text === ''` (line 75) — the exact state produced here — so the intended handling exists but is unreachable on this path. Correct shape: throw an `AiError` (errors.ts already defines the `'safety'` kind and its copy at errors.ts:33) when the accumulated text is empty, or return a tagged result the caller must destructure. Blast radius: 1 call site (ChatModal.tsx:61).

findings.title: No fixture passes a non-object to toAiError(error: unknown), which throws on null/undefined via an unguarded as-cast
findings.description:
Every fixture in this file constructs a real `Error`: `apiError()` on lines 4-6, `new MissingKeyError()`, `new TypeError(...)`, `new SyntaxError(...)`. Nothing ever passes `null`, `undefined`, a bare string or a number — the values `toAiError(error: unknown)` explicitly declares it accepts.

`errors.ts:39-42` does `const status = (error as { status?: unknown }).status;` with no null guard. For `undefined` the flow is: `message = String(undefined)` -> `'undefined'`, which contains none of `quota`/`safety`/`blocked`; not a `SyntaxError`; not a `TypeError`; so it falls to the `else` on line 57 and dereferences `.status` on `undefined` -> `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'status')`. Same for `null`.

`toAiError` is the app's universal error normaliser — every AI entry point wraps its body in `catch (error) { throw toAiError(error) }` (`summarize.ts:56/77/101`, `quiz.ts:19`, and the rest). A function whose entire job is to turn ANYTHING into a friendly `AiError` instead throws a raw `TypeError` for two of the values its own parameter type admits, so instead of a toast the user gets an unhandled rejection. `Promise.reject()` with no argument and `throw undefined` from third-party code both reach it. The `as { status?: unknown }` is the lie: it claims the value is an object.

What goes untested: the non-object branch of a function typed to accept `unknown`.

findings.title: User-controlled book titles are interpolated raw into the prompt that defines the requested output shape
findings.description: `recommendationsPrompt(booksList)` embeds a string that recommend.ts:20-22 builds from `b.title`, `b.author` and `b.category` for every book in the library, unescaped and unlength-capped. Those values are not app-authored: the Goodreads CSV importer writes them verbatim from a file the user supplies, and `Book.title`/`author`/`category` are plain `string` (src/types.ts:31-33) with no branding separating 'text safe to interpolate into a prompt' from 'arbitrary imported text'. The same pattern applies at prompts.ts:24 (detailedSummaryPrompt), :45 (quizPrompt), :56 (chatSystemInstruction) and :81 (audioScript), which additionally interpolate `summary.summary` and `summary.keyInsights` — themselves prior model output. Because line 41 asks in prose for 'strictly JSON with an array of objects containing title, author, and a 1-sentence description', a crafted title can restate or contradict that instruction and steer the response shape; combined with L05-F04's unvalidated cast, a steered response reaches the consumer as a typed `Recommendation[]`. This is adjacent to prompt injection but its type-safety consequence is concrete: the codebase treats a string that controls a request's output contract as interchangeable with a display string. Correct fix shape: escape or fence interpolated library values (and cap their length) in the prompt builders, and keep the runtime validation at the parse site as the real defence. Verified negative worth recording: prompts.ts is otherwise clean — every export has inferred-string return types from template literals, no assertions, no non-null assertions, and the `type: 'short' | 'long'` parameter at line 79 is a proper literal union. Blast radius: 5 prompt builders, all 6 AI entry points.

findings.title: `category` is an unconstrained STRING in the schema, a plain `string` in TS, and the allowed list exists only in prompt prose
findings.description: Three layers disagree about what a category is. The Gemini schema declares `category: { type: Type.STRING }` with no `enum` and no `format: 'enum'`, even though `Schema.enum?: string[]` exists (genai.d.ts:12051). The allowed values live only as prose in prompts.ts:12 ('The category should be one of: Psychology, Productivity, Business, Technology, Philosophy, Health, Biography, Other'), which is a suggestion the model can ignore. `Book.category` (src/types.ts:33) is `string`. And src/types.ts:6-15 declares a `Category` enum with exactly those eight values that is imported and used nowhere in the codebase — dead code that documents an invariant nothing enforces. Failure: the model returns 'Self-Help' or 'Personal Development'; it is accepted, persisted, and LibraryPage.tsx:65 builds the category filter chips from `new Set(books.map(b => b.category))`, so the filter bar accretes near-duplicate one-book categories over time and StatsView's category breakdown fragments. Nothing crashes — this is silent data-quality drift the type system was in a position to prevent. Correct fix: add `enum` + `format: 'enum'` to the schema, change `Book['category']` to a literal union derived from the existing `Category` enum (or delete the enum), and coerce unknown values to 'Other' at the parse boundary — summarize.ts:26 already has the `|| 'Other'` fallback, it just never fires for a non-empty wrong string.

findings.title: `rating` and `readingTimeMinutes` carry their ranges only in description text and are persisted unvalidated
findings.description: Both are `Type.NUMBER` with the intended range stated only in a `description` — 'A rating from 1 to 5' and 'Estimated time in minutes... assume 250 words per minute'. `Schema.minimum`/`Schema.maximum` (genai.d.ts:12064,12072) are available and unused, and `Book.rating` / `Book.readingTimeMinutes` (src/types.ts:36,47) are unbranded `number`s, so neither layer rejects 8.7, -3 or 100000. summarize.ts:28-29 applies only `?? 0` / `?? 5`, which fire on nullish values, not out-of-range ones. AddBookModal.tsx:74 happens to overwrite `rating` with the user's slider value, but LibraryPage.tsx:90-94 (the 'add from recommendation' path) persists the model's number verbatim. Failure: BookCard.tsx:100 renders `{book.rating}/5` producing '8.7/5'; BookDetail.tsx:278-287 renders a five-star row via `num <= Math.round(book.rating)` so a rating of 8.7 lights every star and prints '8.7' beside them; StatsView.tsx:20 averages ratings across finished books and reports a skewed average forever. No crash, but permanently wrong displayed data with no correction path for the rating that came from the recommendation flow. Correct fix: `minimum`/`maximum` in the schema plus a clamp at the parse boundary — the natural home is `toGenerated` in summarize.ts, which already normalises every other field.
