findings.title: The audio part's mimeType is discarded and the PCM format is hardcoded, so a format change produces silently corrupt WAV
findings.description: Line 27 reaches into `response.candidates?.[0]?.content?.parts?.[0]?.inlineData?.data` and takes only `data`. The sibling `inlineData.mimeType` — which Gemini TTS populates with the actual format descriptor, e.g. `audio/L16;codec=pcm;rate=24000` — is never read. `pcmToWavBlob` (src/lib/audio/wav.ts:1-3,12) hardcodes SAMPLE_RATE 24000, NUM_CHANNELS 1, BITS_PER_SAMPLE 16 and stamps those into the RIFF header at wav.ts:22-27. Nothing at any layer checks that the bytes actually match: `base64ToBytes` returns `Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>` for any decodable input and the header is written unconditionally. If a model revision returns a different sample rate or channel count, the WAV header lies about the payload and the audio plays at the wrong pitch and speed — a silent wrong-output failure, not an exception, and the blob is then persisted to the `blobs` store and replayed from cache. The declared parameter type `Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>` describes the container but carries no information about the encoding it must be, which is exactly the case for a branded/validated boundary. Correct fix: read `mimeType` alongside `data`, parse the `rate=` and `codec=` parameters, and either pass them into `pcmToWavBlob` or throw an `AiError` of kind `'malformed'` when they differ from what the WAV writer assumes. Verified positive worth recording: line 28's `if (!base64Audio) throw` correctly narrows the SDK's optional chain instead of using `!` — this file contains no non-null assertion. Blast radius: 2 call sites (BookDetail.tsx:159, EReader.tsx:203).

findings.title: pcmToWavBlob stamps a hardcoded 24kHz/mono/16-bit header on unvalidated Gemini bytes while discarding the mimeType the API actually returns
findings.description:
The signature `pcmToWavBlob(pcm: Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>): Blob` is type-correct but encodes a format contract that only a JSDoc comment asserts ('Gemini TTS returns headerless 24kHz mono 16-bit PCM'). SAMPLE_RATE, NUM_CHANNELS and BITS_PER_SAMPLE are module constants (lines 1-3) written into the header unconditionally. `Uint8Array` says nothing about sample rate, channel count, bit depth, or even that the byte count is even — which it must be for 16-bit mono, since an odd length yields a `data` chunk size that is not a multiple of `blockAlign` (2) and therefore a malformed final sample frame.

The bytes are unvalidated external data. `src/lib/ai/tts.ts:27` reads `response.candidates?.[0]?.content?.parts?.[0]?.inlineData?.data` and line 30 pipes it through `base64ToBytes` straight into `pcmToWavBlob`. Critically, the SDK's `inlineData` is `{ data?: string; displayName?: string; mimeType?: string }` (`node_modules/@google/genai/dist/genai.d.ts:1239-1247`) — the authoritative format IS returned by the API as `mimeType` (e.g. `audio/L16;rate=24000`), and the code discards it in favour of three hardcoded constants.

Failure mode is the dangerous kind: no exception, silently corrupt output. If Gemini ever returns a different rate or bit depth (a model or default change, a different voice pipeline), the header mislabels the stream and the browser plays the audio at the wrong speed and pitch, or as noise. Nothing in the type system, and nothing at runtime, would flag it.

Correct behaviour: read `inlineData.mimeType`, parse the declared rate/encoding, and either build the header from it or reject a stream that does not match the expected format; and reject an odd `pcm.length` for 16-bit audio.

VERIFIED NEGATIVE on the header arithmetic — I checked all 44 bytes against the RIFF/WAVE spec and they are correct: 'RIFF' at 0; ChunkSize `36 + pcm.length` at 4; 'WAVE' at 8; 'fmt ' (with trailing space) at 12; Subchunk1Size 16 at 16; AudioFormat 1 at 20; NumChannels 1 at 22; SampleRate 24000 at 24; ByteRate 48000 at 28 (= 24000*1*2); BlockAlign 2 at 32 (= 1*2); BitsPerSample 16 at 34; 'data' at 36; Subchunk2Size `pcm.length` at 40. All little-endian. `pcm.length` equals `byteLength` for a `Uint8Array`, so the two size fields are right. There are also NO type assertions anywhere in this file, and the parameter is correctly narrowed to `Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>` rather than asserting `as ArrayBuffer` over an `ArrayBufferLike`.

Blast radius: one call site (`src/lib/ai/tts.ts:30`), but it is the whole audio-summary feature.

findings.title: relativeLuminance accepts any string and returns NaN or a plausible wrong number, defeating the project's own WCAG guardrail
findings.description:
`relativeLuminance(hex: string): number` accepts any `string` and declares it always yields a `number`. There is no format validation: `hex.replace('#','')` then `parseInt(slice, 16)` on three fixed slices. Verified at runtime against real inputs:

- `'white'`, `'rgb(255,255,255)'`, `'var(--x)'`, `'oklch(0.7 0.2 40)'`, `''` and 4-digit `#RGBA` shorthand `'#f00a'` all produce `NaN` channels -> `relativeLuminance` returns `NaN` -> `contrastRatio` returns `NaN`.
- Worse, a 5-digit typo `'#12345'` produces NO NaN at all: `parseInt('5', 16)` = 5, so it returns a confident, plausible, wrong luminance (0.0260) and a wrong ratio (1.519 vs `#000000`). A one-character typo in a colour token yields a silently wrong pass/fail verdict with no signal whatsoever.

Why it matters specifically here: CLAUDE.md designates this file as the project's WCAG AA guardrail ('src/lib/contrast.ts exists to assert colour choices meet WCAG AA. Use it when changing colours.'). A guardrail that silently accepts bad input defeats its own purpose. And because `NaN < 4.5` is `false`, any guard written in the natural direction — `if (contrastRatio(fg, bg) < 4.5) fail()` — silently PASSES on unparseable input. The one thing that limits blast radius today is that the module has no production caller: grep shows it is imported only by `src/lib/contrast.test.ts`, and Vitest's `toBeGreaterThanOrEqual` / `toBeLessThan` both fail on NaN, so the current tests would notice. That protection evaporates the moment the module is used in app code or someone writes a guard-style check.

Correct behaviour: parse into `number | null` (or accept a branded `HexColor` produced by one validating constructor) so an unsupported format is a type error or an explicit failure rather than a number. Supporting `#RGBA`/`#RRGGBBAA` and rejecting any other length would close the silent-wrong-value case.

VERIFIED NEGATIVE on the maths itself: the WCAG 2.1 formula is correct — sRGB linearisation threshold 0.03928 with `/12.92` and `((c+0.055)/1.055)**2.4`, coefficients 0.2126/0.7152/0.0722, and `(lighter+0.05)/(darker+0.05)`. `#000000` vs `#ffffff` yields exactly 21. Only the parsing is unsound.

findings.title: Cover lookups declare `Promise<string | null>` but can also reject — the signature lies to new callers
findings.description:
Both exported lookups declare a total contract over `string | null` (src/lib/covers/googleBooks.ts:1 and src/lib/covers/openLibrary.ts:1), but neither is total: `fetch` rejects on any network failure, `response.json()` throws on a non-JSON 200 body, and `url.replace` throws if the L12 cast is wrong (see L06-F01). The declared return type advertises exactly two outcomes when there are three. CORRECT BEHAVIOR: either catch internally and genuinely return `string | null`, or make the throwing contract explicit in the signature/JSDoc so callers cannot miss it.

WHY IT MATTERS: the rejection path is real and proven — src/lib/covers/index.test.ts:53-61 stubs `fetch` to throw and asserts the placeholder fallback. Today the only caller, `fetchCover` (src/lib/covers/index.ts:13-20), wraps both in try/catch, so nothing breaks. But both functions are `export`ed from their modules, and a new caller reading `Promise<string | null>` has no type-level reason to wrap them — the compiler will happily accept `const url = await fetchGoogleBooksCover(t, a); if (url) ...` with no catch, and that call site rejects on the first offline user.

VERIFIED POSITIVE for contrast: the aggregate `fetchCover` in src/lib/covers/index.ts:12 IS honest — it declares `Promise<string>` and genuinely always resolves to a string because L21 falls through to `placeholderCover`. Its caller-side handling is also complete (src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:158 handles the `string | undefined` from `coverForIsbn` with `??`). So the ambiguity is confined to the two provider modules.

BLAST RADIUS: 2 exported functions, 1 current caller each; the risk is entirely forward-looking (new call sites).

findings.title: Google Books HTTP response asserted into a shape with zero runtime validation
findings.description:
`await response.json()` is `any` in lib.dom; the `as {...}` at L12-14 is a pure assertion over a third-party API's live output with no guard, no schema, and no narrowing. The declared shape is fiction: nothing at runtime proves `items` is an array or that `imageLinks` values are strings. CORRECT BEHAVIOR: parse into `unknown` and narrow with a type guard (or validate the picked URL with `typeof url === 'string'`) before use.

CONCRETE FAILURE: the cast declares `imageLinks?: Record<string, string>`, so L24 calls `url.replace(/^http:\/\//, 'https://')` on a value the compiler believes is a `string`. `if (url)` filters null/undefined/'' but NOT a truthy non-string. If the endpoint ever returns a non-string in `imageLinks` (or a differently-shaped 200 body — an error envelope, a captive-portal/proxy interstitial that happens to be valid JSON), `url.replace` is a `TypeError: url.replace is not a function`.

MITIGATION THAT CAPS SEVERITY AT MEDIUM (verified, not assumed): `res.ok` IS checked first at L10 (so 404/500 bodies are never parsed as a success shape — a real positive here), every field is optional-chained, and the sole caller `fetchCover` (src/lib/covers/index.ts:13-20) wraps the call in try/catch and falls through to `placeholderCover`. So today the crash degrades to a placeholder cover, not a user-visible error.

BLAST RADIUS: `fetchCover` <- src/lib/ai/summarize.ts:53 and src/lib/ai/recommend.ts:37 (2 call sites, both AI paths). NOT on the Goodreads import path. This would be HIGH, not medium, the moment anyone calls the exported `fetchGoogleBooksCover` directly without the caller's try/catch (see L06-F04).

findings.title: OpenLibrary search response asserted to `{ docs?: { cover_i?: number }[] }` without validation
findings.description:
Same class as L06-F01: `await response.json()` is `any`, and the `as { docs?: { cover_i?: number }[] }` at L6 asserts a shape over a live third-party API with no runtime check. OpenLibrary's `search.json` returns notoriously sparse and inconsistent records; nothing here proves `docs` is an array or that `cover_i` is a number. CORRECT BEHAVIOR: narrow via `typeof coverId === 'number' && Number.isInteger(coverId)` before building the URL.

CONCRETE FAILURE: if `cover_i` arrives as a string or any other JSON scalar, the cast says `number`, the template at L8 interpolates it regardless, and `Book.coverImageUrl` is persisted to IndexedDB pointing at a URL that 404s. The compiler cannot see it because the assertion told it not to look. There is no crash here (unlike F01) because only string interpolation touches the value — which is why this is medium, not high.

MITIGATION (verified): `res.ok` IS checked at L4 before parsing, `docs?.[0]?.cover_i` is fully optional-chained, and `fetchCover` (src/lib/covers/index.ts:13-20) catches any throw. A bad URL degrades to the `onError` placeholder swap in src/components/BookCard.tsx:18/27.

BLAST RADIUS: reached only via `fetchCover` (2 call sites: src/lib/ai/summarize.ts:53, src/lib/ai/recommend.ts:37).

findings.title: download.test.ts covers only slugify; downloadText has no return annotation and cannot run under the current harness
findings.description:
The module exports two functions. Only `slugify` is tested, and it is tested well (5 cases including the empty-result fallback and the length cap). `downloadText` — the function that actually performs the user-visible export — has zero coverage and cannot be given any without harness work.

`download.ts:2` declares `export function downloadText(filename: string, contents: string, mimeType = 'text/markdown')` with no return type annotation, on an exported symbol. More importantly it calls `URL.createObjectURL` (line 4) and `URL.revokeObjectURL` (line 11). jsdom does not implement either, and `src/test/setup.ts` stubs neither, so any test touching this path dies with `TypeError: URL.createObjectURL is not a function`. `lib.dom` declares both as unconditionally present, so the compiler asserts a capability the test environment does not have — the ambient type is a lie about the runtime the suite runs in.

The same gap blocks three other production call sites: `ProfileView.tsx:99` (library JSON export), `BookDetail.tsx:160` (TTS playback) and `:199` (PDF open), and `EReader.tsx:204`. `useTheme.test.tsx:28` demonstrates the pattern for the analogous `matchMedia` gap by stubbing it per-file rather than in `setup.ts`.

What goes untested: the entire download/blob-URL surface, including the `revokeObjectURL` cleanup that prevents leaked object URLs.

findings.title: coverForIsbn is tested with one perfect ISBN and undefined, so unvalidated ISBN text becomes Book.coverImageUrl
findings.description:
The `coverForIsbn` block has exactly two cases: a clean 13-digit ISBN and `undefined`. `GoodreadsRow.isbn13?: string` is unvalidated free text — `cleanIsbn` at `goodreads.ts:69-72` only strips the Goodreads `="..."` wrapper and returns whatever remains if it is non-empty. `coverForIsbn` then interpolates that directly into a URL and its `string | undefined` return type says nothing about whether the URL resolves.

`useLibrary.tsx:158` writes the result into a `Book`: `coverImageUrl: coverForIsbn(row.isbn13) ?? placeholderCover(row.title)`. Because a bad ISBN still yields a truthy string, the `??` placeholder fallback is bypassed and the book is persisted with a permanently-broken cover URL. Real Goodreads exports produce exactly the inputs no fixture covers: hyphenated ISBNs (`="978-0-7352-1129-2"` -> `covers.openlibrary.org/b/isbn/978-0-7352-1129-2-L.jpg`), 10-digit ISBNs, and placeholder values such as `="0"`. `Book.coverImageUrl: string` claims a usable image URL and delivers an arbitrary string.

What goes untested: every non-canonical ISBN shape, and the interaction that decides whether a Goodreads-imported book gets a real cover or a dead link.

Verified sound in the rest of this file: the `parseGoodreadsCsv` block (lines 10-93) is the strongest suite in the lot — it covers quoted commas, doubled quotes, embedded newlines, CRLF, column reordering, a missing optional column, and the skipped counter. The only gap there is that a blank interior line also increments `skipped` (parseCsv emits a `['']` row, whose empty title takes the skip branch at `goodreads.ts:99-102`), inflating the count shown to the user.

findings.title: Every CSV indexed access is typed as a definite value; the runtime guards are invisible to the compiler
findings.description:
`noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is OFF (tsconfig.json has `strict: true` but not this flag), so in the CSV parser every `array[i]` is typed as a definite value when the runtime value is `undefined` for a short or ragged row. IMPORTANT AND HONEST FRAMING: this file is already correctly guarded at runtime — this is a refactor-safety finding, not a live crash. The unusual value here is that enabling the flag would compile CLEAN on this file, because the guards already exist; it would simply convert them from optional discipline into a compiler-enforced requirement.

ENUMERATED SITES (5, this lot):
- goodreads.ts:29 `const char = text[i]` — typed `string`, would be `string | undefined`; provably in-bounds via the loop condition, so no live bug.
- goodreads.ts:33 `text[i + 1] === '"'` — genuinely `undefined` at the final character; the `===` comparison is safe either way.
- goodreads.ts:82 `(table[0] ?? [])` — guarded by `??`, which the compiler currently believes is unreachable.
- goodreads.ts:96 `(cells[index] ?? '').trim()` — THE ONE THAT MATTERS (see below).
- covers/openLibrary.ts:7 `data.docs?.[0]?.cover_i` — the second `?.` is the only thing handling an empty `docs` array, and the compiler thinks it is redundant.

NAMED CRASH: at L96, for a ragged row — a Goodreads export whose final line is truncated, or any row with fewer commas than the header — `cells[index]` IS `undefined` at runtime while the compiler insists it is `string`. Only the `?? ''` prevents `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'trim')`. That throw would escape `parseGoodreadsCsv`, be caught by src/features/library/GoodreadsImport.tsx:30, and surface as the generic 'Could not read that file.' toast — the user's entire library import fails with no diagnostic. The guard is one character of defensive coding standing between a correct import and total failure, and the type system currently offers zero protection if it is ever deleted as apparently-dead code.

TOOLING NOTE (checked, not assumed): eslint.config.js uses `tseslint.configs.recommended`, NOT `recommendedTypeChecked`/`strictTypeChecked`, so `@typescript-eslint/no-unnecessary-condition` is NOT enabled — no linter will currently flag these `??` guards as dead. The risk is therefore a human or AI reader trusting the declared `string` type, not an automated cleanup.

findings.title: CSV `My Rating` coerced with parseInt and stored unvalidated as an unbounded `number`
findings.description:
`GoodreadsRow.rating` is declared `number` (L7) and produced by `Number.parseInt` over raw file content. The `Number.isFinite` guard at L111 is CORRECT and does kill `NaN` (verified negative — the brief's NaN-propagation hypothesis does not materialise; `Number.isFinite`, not the coercing global `isFinite`, is used). What is missing is any DOMAIN validation: `parseInt` is a lenient parser typed as a total function, so `'-3'` -> -3, `'4.7'` -> 4 (silent truncation), `'12'` -> 12, `'3 stars'` -> 3. All are finite, so all are stored. CORRECT BEHAVIOR: clamp/validate to Goodreads' 0-5 domain at the parse boundary (a `Rating` branded type or a `>= 0 && <= 5` guard), rather than trusting `number`.

CONCRETE FAILURE: the value flows unvalidated to src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:156 -> `bookRepo.create` (src/lib/storage/repo.ts:51, which performs no validation — its param type is just `Omit<Book,'id'|'addedAt'>`) -> IndexedDB. It is then consumed by src/components/StatsView.tsx:20 `(finished.reduce((acc, b) => acc + b.rating, 0) / finished.length).toFixed(1)`, so one out-of-range row silently reports an average like `8.4` on a 5-point scale; and by src/lib/markdown.ts:14 `**Rating:** ${book.rating}/5`, which exports `-3/5` into the user's markdown. src/components/BookDetail.tsx:278 `num <= Math.round(book.rating)` renders all five stars lit for any rating >= 5 and zero for a negative — wrong, but no crash. Because the record is persisted, the corruption survives reload; nothing re-validates on read.

TRIGGER (honest): Goodreads itself only writes 0-5, so the realistic entry point is a hand-edited export or a non-Goodreads CSV that happens to carry a `My Rating` header — a plausible user path, not the default one. Hence medium, not high.

BLAST RADIUS: 4 consumers of `Book.rating` (StatsView, BookDetail, BookCard.tsx:100, markdown.ts).

findings.title: dueAt is a bare string compared numerically by isDue and lexically by repo.listDue, and nothing cross-checks them
findings.description:
`ReviewCard.dueAt` is typed `string` (`types.ts:92`) with the invariant "canonical ISO-8601 UTC timestamp" living only in comments. Two consumers read it with different orderings:
- `srs.ts:58` — `Date.parse(card.dueAt) <= now.getTime()` (numeric, tolerant of any parseable format, yields `NaN` for garbage)
- `repo.ts:88` — `card.dueAt <= cutoff` (lexicographic string compare, correct only for zero-padded, same-offset ISO strings)

The `isDue` block in this file (lines 97-108) only ever feeds `dueAt` values it produced itself via `newCard`/`scheduleCard` or hand-wrote in canonical form. `repo.listDue` has no test at all (see L13-F13). So nothing anywhere pins the two comparisons to the same semantics. A non-padded `'2026-8-12'` is due under `isDue` and not due under `listDue`; `NaN` from an unparseable value makes `isDue` return `false` forever, so the card silently never surfaces again — a card that disappears rather than errors.

The type is the problem: `dueAt: string` lets any string in, and `ease`/`intervalDays` as bare `number`s are the same shape of footgun (`scheduleCard(card, grade)` is safe only because `Grade = 1|2|3|4` is a literal union — that part is done right). A branded `IsoTimestamp` produced by a single helper would make the two comparison sites provably consistent.

Verified sound in this file: `card(overrides)` on lines 7-22 builds from the real `newCard` factory and is annotated `: ReviewCard`, so the compiler enforces completeness — this is the honest-fixture pattern the rest of the suite should copy.

findings.title: dueAt is a bare string whose fixed-width-UTC-ISO invariant is unenforced, and two consumers compare it in incompatible ways
findings.description:
`ReviewCard.dueAt` is typed `string` (`src/types.ts:93`). Both producers in this file happen to write `Date.prototype.toISOString()` output (srs.ts:33 and srs.ts:52), but nothing in the type requires that, and two consumers depend on mutually incompatible readings of the same field:

- `src/lib/storage/repo.ts:88` filters with a LEXICOGRAPHIC compare: `owned.filter((card) => card.dueAt <= cutoff).sort((a, b) => a.dueAt.localeCompare(b.dueAt))`, with the comment 'ISO timestamps sort chronologically, so a string compare is enough'. That is only true for the fixed-width, `Z`-suffixed, 4-digit-year form.
- `src/lib/srs.ts:58` `isDue` uses a SEMANTIC compare: `Date.parse(card.dueAt) <= now.getTime()`.

The two disagree on any other valid timestamp string, and `string` permits all of them. Concrete divergences: an offset form such as `'2026-08-12T10:00:00+02:00'` — a perfectly valid ISO 8601 string that many date libraries emit — parses correctly under `Date.parse` but sorts before every digit under a byte compare (`'+'` is 0x2B, `'2'` is 0x32), so `listDue` would report it due immediately and sort it first, forever. The extended-year form `toISOString()` itself emits for years outside 0000-9999 (`'+275760-09-13T00:00:00.000Z'`) has the same property. Separately, `Date.parse` on an unparseable string returns `NaN`, and `NaN <= x` is `false`, so `isDue` silently answers 'not due' — a card disappears from review permanently with no error, and the `boolean` return type hides that third state.

Compounding this: `isDue` has NO production caller. Grep shows it is imported only by `src/lib/srs.test.ts`; the app uses the string compare in `repo.ts:88` exclusively. So the unit tests validate a due-date predicate the application never runs, while the predicate the application does run is untested against non-canonical input.

Correct behaviour: introduce a branded `IsoUtcTimestamp` (or `Millis`) constructed by one factory, so every producer is forced through the canonicalising path and the lexicographic-sort assumption in `repo.ts` becomes something the type actually guarantees. Then either delete `isDue` or make `repo.ts` use it, so there is one definition of 'due'.

Blast radius: `src/types.ts:93` (`dueAt`), plus every other bare-`string` timestamp field on the same types (`Book.addedAt`, `Book.finishedAt`, `Summary.generatedAt`, `Profile.createdAt`); producers at srs.ts:33,52; consumers at repo.ts:88-89 and srs.ts:58.

findings.title: scheduleCard declares a total return of ReviewCard but throws RangeError once ease/interval go non-finite; ease has a floor and no ceiling
findings.description:
`scheduleCard(card, grade, now): ReviewCard` cannot produce a `ReviewCard` for every input it accepts. Line 52 calls `new Date(now.getTime() + intervalDays * DAY_MS).toISOString()`, which throws `RangeError: Invalid time value` whenever the argument is `NaN` or outside the +/-8.64e15 ms Date range. Verified at runtime: `new Date(NaN).toISOString()` and `new Date(Infinity).toISOString()` both throw.

Two reachable triggers, both invisible to the compiler because `ease`, `intervalDays` and `reviewCount` are bare `number` on `ReviewCard` (`src/types.ts:91-94`):

1. Unbounded ease. `EASE_DELTA[4] = 0.1` and line 43 applies only a floor (`Math.max(MIN_EASE, ...)`) — there is no `MAX_EASE`. Ease therefore grows without limit, and line 46 multiplies the interval by `ease * 1.3` each time. Simulated: after 14 consecutive grade-4 ('Easy') reviews, `ease = 3.9` and `intervalDays = 480,395,074` (~1.3 million years), at which point `now + intervalDays * DAY_MS` exceeds the Date range and line 52 throws. Standard SM-2 caps ease; this implementation does not.
2. Non-finite input. `Math.max(1.3, NaN)` returns `NaN` and `Math.max(1, NaN)` returns `NaN` (both verified), so a single non-finite `card.ease` or `card.intervalDays` propagates straight through the floor guards into line 52. `ReviewCard` values are read back from IndexedDB via `getDb().getAll('reviewCards')` (`src/lib/storage/repo.ts:79,95`) where the `idb` DBSchema typing is a compile-time claim over rows with zero runtime validation.

Caller impact: `src/features/review/useReviewQueue.ts:38` calls `await cardRepo.upsert(scheduleCard(current, gradeValue))` inside an async `useCallback` with no try/catch. A throw becomes an unhandled rejection: the grade button appears to do nothing, the card is never rescheduled, and the queue never advances — the review session dead-ends with no error surfaced.

Correct behaviour: cap ease (`MIN_EASE <= ease <= MAX_EASE`), clamp `intervalDays` to a sane maximum (e.g. 10 years), and express these as refined/branded numeric types constructed through one validating factory so the invariants are not re-implemented per call site. Alternatively make the return type honest about failure.

Blast radius: the single scheduling function behind the entire review feature; one call site (`useReviewQueue.ts:38`) but it is the only write path for review scheduling.

findings.title: DBSchema value types promise every read row is a valid domain object, but IndexedDB validates nothing on the way out
findings.description: `BookSumDB` declares `books: { value: Book }`, `summaries: { value: Summary }` and so on, which makes `idb` type every read as `Book | undefined`, `Summary | undefined` etc. That is a guarantee IndexedDB structurally cannot provide: `db.get('books', id)` returns whatever object was structured-cloned in, by whatever code version wrote it, with zero shape checking. Today this is not merely theoretical — it is the read side of L02-F01. `src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:111` writes unvalidated objects from a user-supplied backup file into the `books` store, so the store genuinely can contain rows that are not `Book`s, and every subsequent `books.get` / `books.listByProfile` (`src/lib/storage/repo.ts:44,47`) hands them to callers stamped as valid. Note the compounding factor: `DB_VERSION` is 1 and the `upgrade` handler (db.ts:24-39) only ever runs the create-store path — it ignores the `oldVersion` argument `idb` supplies and contains no row-reshaping step, so there is no mechanism by which a malformed or older-shaped row would ever be repaired. The declared types are the app's only defence and they are compile-time only. Correct shape: keep the `DBSchema` value types as the intended shape, but treat `repo.ts` as the trust boundary — validate (or at least normalise required fields on) rows entering the store from any external source, so the type on the way out is earned rather than asserted.

findings.title: blobs store key is a composite `${bookId}:${kind}` but is declared plain string, identical to the by-book index key
findings.description: The `blobs` store's primary key is not an id — it is a composite built by `src/lib/storage/repo.ts:126` (`const blobKey = (bookId: string, kind: BlobKind) => `${bookId}:${kind}``). The schema declares it as bare `string`, and the same store's `by-book` index key is also `string` but holds a raw `bookId`. Two structurally different key spaces are therefore the same type inside one store declaration, so `db.get('blobs', someBookId)` type-checks perfectly and simply returns `undefined` — a silent miss indistinguishable from 'no PDF stored', which in this app means the reader renders nothing rather than reporting an error. No current call site is wrong (repo.ts consistently routes through `blobKey`, and repo.ts:149-150 correctly feeds `getAllKeysFromIndex` results back to `delete`), so this is a latent footgun rather than a live bug — but it is a cheap one to close. Correct shape: `key: `${string}:${BlobKind}`` (a template-literal type, no runtime branding needed) — `blobKey()` already produces exactly that, so the only change is the declaration, and passing a bare bookId stops compiling. Two related observations from checking this store: `StoredBlob` (src/types.ts:67-80) also lets `key`, `bookId` and `kind` disagree with one another even though `repo.ts:133-139` always derives `key` from the other two; and every other declared index key type in this schema was verified correct against its `keyPath` (`by-profile` -> `profileId`, `by-book` -> `bookId`, `by-profile-due` -> `['profileId','dueAt']`), though `by-profile-due` is never actually queried since repo.ts:79 and :95 both do a full-store `getAll` and filter in memory.

findings.title: keyInsights/actionableSteps defaulted with ?? [] are declared string[] but a non-array legacy value survives
findings.description: `legacy.keyInsights ?? []` only replaces null/undefined. A legacy record holding a string, an object, or a comma-joined value is written straight into `Summary.keyInsights: string[]`. Consumers call array methods on it with no guard: src/lib/markdown.ts:24-25 does `.length > 0` then `.map(...)` (a string passes the length check and then throws `TypeError: ... .map is not a function`, breaking the export-to-markdown feature), and src/lib/ai/prompts.ts:36, 49, 67 and 82 call `.join(...)` on both fields when building the summarise/deep-dive/TTS prompts, which throws before the AI request is made. `detailedSummary: legacy.detailedSummary` at line 129 is passed with no check at all. Blast radius: every migrated summary; 6 summaries.* call sites plus the markdown export and four prompt builders. Correct behaviour: `Array.isArray(x) ? x.filter(i => typeof i === 'string') : []` at the migration boundary, so the declared string[] is true by construction.

findings.title: base64ToBytes is handed a value only declared to be a string, on the unguarded boot path
findings.description: `legacy.pdfData` and `legacy.audioData` are declared `string?` by the LegacyBook interface but originate from the unvalidated JSON.parse of L03-F01. The truthiness guards at lines 135 and 141 filter nullish/empty but not type or content. src/lib/base64.ts:6 then calls `atob(base64)`, which throws `InvalidCharacterError` for any string that is not valid base64 - including a legacy value that was truncated by a localStorage quota failure, which is precisely how large base64 PDFs failed in the original app (CLAUDE.md: 'No binary data in records... This is what broke the original app'). Because migrateLegacyData() is awaited unguarded at ProfileContext.tsx:31 and the MIGRATION_MARKER is only written at line 149, one bad pdfData string permanently blocks app boot - the same brick as L03-F01. Blast radius: one throw aborts the entire migration for every profile, and the partial writes already made are not rolled back. Correct behaviour: check `typeof x === 'string'` plus a base64 shape test (or wrap the decode per-record) so a single unreadable attachment is skipped rather than fatal.

findings.title: The cascade test omits reviewCards, and the whole reviewCards store surface is untested
findings.description:
`removes the summary and blobs when a book is removed` asserts three things after `books.remove`: the book is gone, the summary is gone, the blob is gone. It does not assert that review cards are gone, even though `repo.ts:72` calls `reviewCards.removeByBook(id)` in that same cascade and `ReviewCard` rows carry a `bookId` foreign key. The profile-level cascade test on lines 88-97 has the same omission. Nothing in `repo.test.ts` touches `reviewCards` at all — `listByProfile`, `listDue`, `listByBook`, `upsert` and `removeByBook` (repo.ts:77-109) have zero coverage in the module's own suite.

That matters for type honesty because `reviewCards.listByProfile` and `listByBook` are raw `getDb().getAll('reviewCards')` reads typed solely by the `BookSumDB` schema declaration at `db.ts:12-16`. Nothing validates that a stored row is actually a `ReviewCard`; the declaration is an assertion about the contents of a store the app has been writing to since v1. Orphaned cards from a book deleted before the cascade existed would be returned as `ReviewCard[]` and fed to the review UI with a `bookId` that resolves to nothing.

More generally, every read test in this file is a closed loop: the suite writes with `profiles.create`/`books.create`, then reads back with `profiles.list`/`books.listByProfile`. No fixture ever puts a record into the store that the repo did not itself construct, so the schema's type claims can never be falsified. `profiles.list` at `repo.ts:9` does `a.createdAt.localeCompare(b.createdAt)` — an unguarded dereference on a field that only the repo's own writer guarantees.

findings.title: profiles.update and books.update write whatever the caller hands them, persisting NaN as a typed number
findings.description: Both update methods are a straight pass-through to put() with no validation - the record's correctness rests entirely on the caller's static type. That is not sufficient because a value can satisfy `number` and still be garbage: src/components/ProfileView.tsx:239 sets `monthlyGoal: parseInt(e.target.value)`, and parseInt('') is NaN, which is a `number` as far as the compiler is concerned. Clearing the monthly-goal field and saving persists `Profile.monthlyGoal = NaN` through repo.ts:31. ProfileView.tsx:53 then computes `Math.min(100, (finishedCount / NaN) * 100)` = NaN and renders a NaN-width progress bar. The corruption also outlives the session: structured clone preserves NaN in IndexedDB, and JSON.stringify in the backup export turns it into null, so a subsequent import writes `monthlyGoal: null` under a `number` declaration. Blast radius: 26 profiles.* and 22 books.* call sites read records these two methods can poison. Correct behaviour: the repo's write boundary should reject non-finite numbers and empty required strings rather than trusting the declared type.

findings.title: Every identifier in the persistence API is a bare string, including two adjacent methods that take different id kinds
findings.description: profileId, bookId, summaryId and blobKey are all `string`, so the compiler cannot tell them apart anywhere in the repo's public surface. The sharpest foot-gun is inside `summaries`: getByBook(bookId) at line 112 and remove(id) at line 121 are seven lines apart and take different kinds of id with identical types. books.remove at 68-73 gets it right (`summaries.getByBook(id)` then `summaries.remove(summary.id)`), but `summaries.remove(id)` with the book id compiles cleanly and silently deletes nothing - an orphaned summary that later collides with a regenerated one. Same exposure for blobKey(bookId, kind) at line 126 (a summaryId compiles and produces a key that will never match), reviewCards.removeByBook(bookId) vs the card ids deleted at line 107, and books.create's input where profileId and the optional id are both string. Related: StoredBlob.key is documented as `${bookId}:${kind}` (types.ts:68) but declared `string`, where a template-literal type would enforce the format blobKey produces. Blast radius: every exported repo method except blobs.put takes at least one bare-string id - 75+ call sites across src pass ids positionally. Correct behaviour: branded id types (BookId, ProfileId, SummaryId) minted at creation, which is a moderate but mechanical retrofit since all ids originate from newId() at line 4.

findings.title: setup.ts provides no typed fetch stub, so four hand-rolled stubs diverge from typeof fetch and one leaks across tests
findings.description:
`setup.ts` wires jest-dom, fake-indexeddb, an `asyncUtilTimeout` and an `afterEach` cleanup — but no shared browser-API stubbing. Every suite that needs `fetch` hand-rolls its own, and `vi.stubGlobal(name, value: unknown)` accepts anything, so the compiler never checks any of them against `typeof globalThis.fetch`. Four divergent stubs result:
- `smoke.test.tsx:43` — `(input: RequestInfo | URL) => Promise<Response>`, drops the `init` parameter entirely
- `covers/index.test.ts:8` — same, drops `init`
- `covers/index.test.ts:56` — `async () => { throw ... }`, zero parameters, inferred `Promise<never>`
- `covers/index.test.ts:64` — drops `init` again
Dropping `init` means any production `fetch(url, { signal, headers, method })` has its options silently discarded under test, and any assertion written over `call[1]` would be untypeable. Real `fetch` returns `Promise<Response>` and can reject; the `Promise<never>` stub is not assignable to it and nothing says so.

Second, concrete consequence of there being no shared helper: `smoke.test.tsx:61` calls `vi.unstubAllGlobals()` as the last statement of the test BODY rather than in an `afterEach`. `restoreMocks: true` in `vite.config.ts:24` restores spies but does not undo `stubGlobal`, and `unstubGlobals` is not set. If any assertion between lines 49 and 60 fails, the stubbed `fetch` — which answers every request with a fixed 200 `{}` — leaks into the two later tests in the same file, silently changing what they exercise. `covers/index.test.ts:16-18` gets this right with an `afterEach`; nothing enforces the difference.

The fix shape is a single typed helper in `setup.ts` (`stubFetch(fn: typeof globalThis.fetch)`) plus `unstubGlobals: true`, which restores the compiler check and centralises teardown. Also absent: any stub for `URL.createObjectURL`/`revokeObjectURL` (see L13-F10).

findings.title: The 'no Gemini call on boot' invariant is asserted by a for-loop that runs zero times when nothing is captured
findings.description:
`makes no network call to Gemini on boot` guards one of CLAUDE.md's stated invariants, and its entire assertion is a `for` loop over `fetchSpy.mock.calls`. If `mock.calls` is empty the loop body never executes and the test passes having asserted nothing at all. There is no `expect(fetchSpy).toHaveBeenCalled()`, no `expect.assertions(n)`, and no check that the spy was actually installed in the path under test.

That makes the test indistinguishable between three outcomes: (a) boot genuinely made no request — the intended pass; (b) boot made requests through a `fetch` reference captured at module-import time, before `vi.stubGlobal` ran on line 47, so the spy never saw them; (c) a future refactor moves the network call somewhere the spy does not cover. Only (a) is the invariant; all three are green.

The stub also returns a fixed `new Response('{}', { status: 200 })` for every URL, so even if a Gemini call happened it would be answered successfully rather than surfacing as a failure. The identical pattern is at `covers/index.test.ts:72-74` (`never calls a Gemini endpoint`), where the loop does currently run — but nothing keeps it that way.

What goes untested: whether the spy is on the path at all. The cheap fix is asserting a non-zero call count (or `expect.hasAssertions()`) alongside the URL check.

findings.title: ISO-8601 timestamps are bare strings whose format is load-bearing for sorting, and one is piped in unvalidated from localStorage
findings.description: `Profile.createdAt`, `Book.addedAt`, `Book.finishedAt`, `Summary.generatedAt` and `ReviewCard.dueAt` are all `string`, but their ISO-8601 format is load-bearing rather than cosmetic: `src/lib/storage/repo.ts:9` orders the profile list with `a.createdAt.localeCompare(b.createdAt)` and `repo.ts:88-89` selects the review queue with `card.dueAt <= cutoff` — lexicographic comparisons that are only correct because ISO-8601 happens to sort chronologically (the code comments say so at repo.ts:83). A bare `string` gives the compiler no way to enforce that. The live ingress is `src/lib/storage/migrate.ts:95`, which pipes `legacyProfile?.joinedAt` — an arbitrary string from `JSON.parse` of localStorage, obtained through the `readJson<T>` assertion at migrate.ts:54-62 — directly into `profiles.create({ createdAt })`, and `repo.ts:24` stores it verbatim (`input.createdAt ?? new Date().toISOString()`). A legacy profile carrying `joinedAt: 'March 3, 2024'` is therefore persisted as a `Profile.createdAt` that sorts before every ISO timestamp forever, silently reordering the profile picker with no error. A second symptom of the missing type: the same `dueAt` field is interpreted two different ways by two modules — `repo.ts:89` compares it as a string while `src/lib/srs.ts:58` does `Date.parse(card.dueAt) <= now.getTime()`. Correct shape: a branded `IsoDateString` produced by one factory that validates on construction, so the migration path is forced to parse-and-normalise `joinedAt` instead of passing it through.

findings.title: Book/Summary/Profile/ReviewCard ids are all bare string, and one adjacent-line call site would silently swallow a swap
findings.description: Every entity id in the domain model is `string`: `Book.id`/`Book.profileId`/`Book.summaryId`, `Summary.id`/`Summary.bookId`, `Profile.id`, `ReviewCard.id`/`profileId`/`bookId`. The repo signatures are correspondingly indistinguishable — `books.get(id: string)`, `books.remove(id: string)`, `summaries.remove(id: string)` (a summary id) and `profiles.get(id: string)` all accept any of them. The concrete swap-compiles site is `src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:81-83`, where three different id kinds are juggled across three adjacent lines: `const book = await bookRepo.get(summary.bookId); if (book && book.summaryId !== summary.id) await bookRepo.update({ ...book, summaryId: summary.id })`. Writing `bookRepo.get(summary.id)` instead of `bookRepo.get(summary.bookId)` type-checks, returns `undefined`, and the very next line's `if (book && ...)` guard swallows it — the summary/book link is silently never written, with no throw and no log, and the book keeps rendering as unsummarised. `reviewCards.listByProfile(profileId: string)` and `reviewCards.listByBook(bookId: string)` (repo.ts:78, 94) likewise have identical signatures and different meanings. Correct shape: branded aliases (`type BookId = string & { readonly __brand: 'BookId' }`, etc.) applied at the `types.ts` declarations and threaded through the repo signatures; per the audit spec this is a retrofit cost, so prioritise `BookId` vs `SummaryId` (the pair with a demonstrated silent-failure path) over the rest.

findings.title: Book.category is an unconstrained string fed by the LLM, while the Category enum declared right above it is dead code
findings.description: `types.ts:6-15` exports a `Category` enum with eight members, and `types.ts:33` then declares `Book.category` as bare `string`. A search across `src/` finds no reference to the `Category` identifier anywhere outside its own declaration — the only other hits are unrelated JSX label text and `activeCategory` locals — so the enum is dead and the field it was written for is unconstrained. Producers write free-form strings: `'Other'` at `src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:154`, `src/lib/storage/migrate.ts:109` and `src/lib/ai/summarize.ts:26`, and otherwise whatever Gemini returns, since `src/lib/ai/schemas.ts:8` declares `category: { type: Type.STRING }` with no enum constraint and `RawBookResponse.category?: string` is asserted straight out of `JSON.parse` at summarize.ts:52. Consumers then compare that string exactly: `src/features/library/LibraryPage.tsx:47` filters with `book.category === activeCategory`, and `src/components/StatsView.tsx:23-28` builds the entire Category Breakdown chart by grouping on the raw string. Concrete failure: the model returns 'Self-Help' for one book and 'self-help' for another; the stats chart shows them as two separate categories with a count of 1 each, and the library filter chip for one will never match the other. Correct behaviour: type `Book.category` as the `Category` enum (or a string-literal union) and normalise the AI-supplied value against that set at the `summarize.ts` boundary, falling back to `Other` — the enum to do it with already exists.

findings.title: Book.hasPdf is a denormalised copy of blob-store existence that the caller must state twice, unchecked
findings.description: `hasPdf: boolean` duplicates a fact that already lives in the `blobs` store (is there a row keyed `${id}:pdf`). Because the two are unrelated at the type level, the `addBook` API forces the caller to assert the same fact twice in two different arguments and never checks that they agree: `src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:50-51` stores the blob if `options.pdf` is set, while `hasPdf` arrives independently on the draft. `src/components/AddBookModal.tsx:76` happens to derive both from the same local (`hasPdf: Boolean(pdf)` on line 76, `pdf` passed in options on line 78), so the two agree by convention rather than by construction — and the test suite shows how awkward this is, with `src/features/library/useLibrary.test.tsx:109` having to hand-write `api.addBook({ ...draft(), hasPdf: true }, { pdf: new Blob(['x']) })`. Concrete failure: `addBook({ ...draft, hasPdf: false }, { pdf: someBlob })` compiles cleanly and produces a book whose PDF bytes are sitting in IndexedDB but are permanently unreachable, because `src/components/BookDetail.tsx:196` returns early on `if (!book.hasPdf) return;` and `:402` gates the reader entry point on `{book.hasPdf && ...}`. The user sees no PDF, no error, and the orphaned bytes keep consuming quota. Correct shape: model the PDF-bearing case as a union arm (or drop the boolean and derive it from the blob store at read time), so the flag and the blob cannot be supplied independently.

findings.title: ReviewCard.correctAnswerIndex has no type-level relation to options, and out-of-range LLM values are persisted permanently
findings.description: `options: string[]` and `correctAnswerIndex: number` sit adjacent with no expressed relationship, so `correctAnswerIndex` may legally be any number including one outside the array. The value originates from Gemini (`src/lib/ai/schemas.ts:69-72`, where 'Index (0-3) of the correct answer' is only a natural-language description in the prompt schema, not a checked constraint), enters via the `QuizQuestion` cast in `src/lib/ai/quiz.ts:16`, and is copied verbatim with no bounds check by `src/lib/srs.ts:29` (`correctAnswerIndex: input.correctAnswerIndex`) into a `ReviewCard` that is then written to IndexedDB. Unlike a transient render bug this corruption is durable. Concrete failure: the model returns `correctAnswerIndex: 4` for a 4-element `options` array; `src/features/review/ReviewPage.tsx:76` evaluates `selected === current.correctAnswerIndex` which can never be true for any of the four rendered buttons, and `:94` (`index === current.correctAnswerIndex`) never highlights a correct answer either. The user cannot pass the card, so `scheduleCard` keeps failing it, the SRS interval resets to 1 day (`src/lib/srs.ts:46`), and the broken card resurfaces in the due queue every single day forever with no way to fix it from the UI. Correct behaviour: validate `correctAnswerIndex` against `options.length` at the `quiz.ts` boundary before a card is ever created, and drop or repair questions that fail. The type itself cannot express the bound, which is exactly why the runtime check has to exist.

findings.title: LibraryExport.version is a literal tag that no consumer ever narrows on, so older backups import as v2
findings.description: `version: 2` is a literal type, so from the compiler's point of view every `LibraryExport` in the program is definitionally version 2 and a version check would be flagged as a redundant comparison. That is only true for values the app itself produces (`src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:94` writes `version: 2`). For values that come off disk it is fiction — `src/components/ProfileView.tsx:117` asserts an arbitrary parsed file into the type, and `importLibrary` (useLibrary.tsx:102-122) never reads `payload.version` at all. The one field explicitly designed as a schema discriminant is therefore load-bearing for nothing. Concrete failure: a user restores a version-1 backup produced by an older build (the `version: 2` literal and the interface name imply a v1 existed); it has a `books` array so it clears the `Array.isArray` check at ProfileView.tsx:119, and every row is merged into the library under v2 assumptions with no migration and no warning. Correct shape: make `LibraryExport` an actual discriminated union over `version` (or at minimum `version: number` plus an explicit runtime check that rejects or upgrades anything that is not 2) so the tag can narrow and unsupported versions fail loudly instead of importing silently.

findings.title: noUncheckedIndexedAccess is off — 10 real unchecked-index sites, several on rendered UI paths
findings.description:
`strict: true` is set but `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is not, so every array index and index-signature read is typed as `T` when the runtime can produce `undefined`. Measured empirically: `npx tsc --noEmit --noUncheckedIndexedAccess` produces exactly 10 errors across 4 files (baseline is 0).

The worst cluster is `src/components/QuizModal.tsx` (5 errors), where `questions[currentQuestionIndex]` is dereferenced on the render path at lines 178, 182, 183 and 232 and in the click handler at line 78 — e.g. `questions[currentQuestionIndex].correctAnswerIndex`. `questions` is AI-generated content and `currentQuestionIndex` is React state, so the compiler currently cannot prove the pair is in range; a quiz response with fewer questions than expected, or a state update ordering bug, is a `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined` in render. `src/components/BookDetail.tsx` (3) and `src/components/AddBookModal.tsx`/`EReader.tsx` (1 each) are the remainder.

Correct behaviour: enable the flag and resolve each site with a narrowing guard or a destructured local, not with `!`. Adoption cost is genuinely low here — 10 errors in 4 files, all in component code, no library or storage churn.

Important interaction: see L01-F04. `@typescript-eslint/no-non-null-assertion` is currently off, so the cheapest way to silence all 10 of these errors is to append `!`, which converts a compile-time gap into a runtime crash. Enable the lint rule in the same change, or this flag makes things worse.

findings.title: exactOptionalPropertyTypes is off — 9 sites write explicit `undefined` into `?:` fields persisted to IndexedDB
findings.description:
`exactOptionalPropertyTypes` is not enabled, so a field declared `priority?: Priority` silently accepts an explicit `priority: undefined`. Measured: `npx tsc --noEmit --exactOptionalPropertyTypes` produces exactly 9 errors across 7 files.

This matters more than usual in this codebase because the offending sites are the paths that build records for IndexedDB, where "key absent" and "key present with value undefined" are not the same thing — they differ on `in` checks, `Object.keys` length, structured-clone round-trips, index population, and JSON export shape. The affected producers are `src/lib/storage/migrate.ts` (3 errors: `Profile`, `Book` and `Summary` construction at lines 90, 105, 122), `src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:45` (`summaryId`/`oneSentenceTakeaway`), `src/lib/goodreads.ts:107` (`isbn13`, `dateRead` from CSV), and `src/components/AddBookModal.tsx:70` (`priority`). Two more are in `src/lib/markdown.test.ts` (lines 60, 84) where fixtures pass `personalNotes: undefined` and `summary: undefined` — per the audit spec these are the higher-value ones, because the fixture shape differs from the production record shape the code claims to handle.

Correct behaviour: decide per field whether it is genuinely optional (`?:`, omit the key) or nullable-but-present (`: T | undefined`), then enable the flag. Adoption cost is moderate rather than trivial — it is only 9 errors, but each is a deliberate modelling decision on a persisted type, and `Book`/`Profile`/`Summary` are shared by many consumers.

findings.title: noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature is off, masking a lying `Record<string, string>` on the Google Books boundary
findings.description:
`noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature` is not enabled. Measured: `npx tsc --noEmit --noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature` produces exactly 5 errors, and all 5 are in one file — `src/lib/covers/googleBooks.ts` lines 19-23.

The flag itself is a style guard, but here it points at a genuine lying type at an external-API boundary. `src/lib/covers/googleBooks.ts:12-14` casts the Google Books response to `{ items?: { volumeInfo?: { imageLinks?: Record<string, string> } }[] }`. Because `imageLinks` is `Record<string, string>`, the compiler believes every key maps to a present `string`. So in the fallback chain at lines 19-23, `links?.extraLarge` is typed `string | undefined` only because `links` itself may be undefined — the compiler considers the `?? links?.large ?? ... ?? links?.smallThumbnail` tail unreachable whenever `links` exists. In reality the Google Books API commonly returns only `thumbnail` and `smallThumbnail`, so the fallbacks are the hot path. The types describe the opposite of the runtime.

Correct behaviour: replace `Record<string, string>` with an explicit optional-keyed interface (`{ extraLarge?: string; large?: string; medium?: string; thumbnail?: string; smallThumbnail?: string }`), which makes the `??` chain honest and makes these 5 errors disappear without enabling anything. Enabling `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` (L01-F02) would independently make the index reads honest, and notably adds zero errors here because the `??` chain already handles undefined. Adoption cost: trivial, one file, one type.

findings.title: reviewCards read path loads every row unvalidated and sorts on dueAt with a string method
findings.description: listByProfile and listByBook call `getAll('reviewCards')` - fetching every card of every profile - and immediately access `card.profileId` / `card.bookId` on rows typed only by db.ts:12-16. listDue then does `card.dueAt <= cutoff` and `a.dueAt.localeCompare(b.dueAt)` at line 89: a non-string dueAt makes the comparison at line 88 silently false (the card never becomes due, so it disappears from the review queue with no error) and, if it survives the filter, makes localeCompare throw. Note the cross-profile read also means one profile's corrupt card can break another profile's review session. Blast radius: 10 reviewCards.* call sites; the review queue is the whole of the Phase 3 feature. Correct behaviour: validate dueAt as an ISO string at the boundary, and prefer the existing 'by-profile-due' index over an unvalidated full-table scan.

findings.title: summaries.getByBook returns an unverified index hit typed Summary, whose array fields are consumed without guards
findings.description: `getFromIndex('summaries', 'by-book', bookId)` is typed `Summary | undefined` from db.ts:10. The undefined half is honest (callers do check it - repo.ts:69-70 and BookDetail both guard), but the Summary half is a declaration, not a check. Whatever is on disk is handed to consumers that immediately call array and string methods on its fields: src/lib/markdown.ts:22-28 and src/lib/ai/prompts.ts:36-82. Records written by summaries.upsert (repo.ts:116, itself unvalidated - see L03-F04) or by the migration (L03-F10) can violate the declared shape, and the mismatch surfaces as a TypeError inside markdown export or prompt construction rather than at the read. Blast radius: 6 summaries.* call sites, feeding the book detail view, the markdown export, the quiz generator and all AI prompt builders. Correct behaviour: validate at this boundary so the failure is attributable to the bad record, not to the consumer three modules away.

findings.title: The stored MIME type is an unconstrained string, uncoupled from BlobKind, and is replayed into a same-origin blob: URL
findings.description: blobs.put writes `type: blob.type` verbatim at line 138 and blobs.get replays it into the reconstructed Blob at line 144. The repo already knows the BlobKind ('pdf' | 'audio-short' | 'audio-long'), so the MIME type is derivable and checkable, yet StoredBlob.type is declared as an open `string` with no relationship to kind - a 'pdf' record can legitimately carry any MIME string as far as the types are concerned. The write source is a user-picked File (src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:51, from the AddBookModal.tsx:232 input whose `accept=".pdf"` is a dialog hint, not enforcement), so blob.type is whatever the browser derived from the chosen file. On read, src/components/BookDetail.tsx:199-200 does `URL.createObjectURL(pdf)` then `window.open(url, '_blank')`; a blob: URL inherits the creating document's origin, so a stored `text/html` type means script executing in the app's origin with access to the Gemini API key that CLAUDE.md keeps in localStorage. Blast radius: 17 blobs.* call sites; the type string is written in exactly one place and read in exactly one place, so the fix is contained. Correct behaviour: derive or allow-list the MIME per BlobKind at the repo boundary instead of round-tripping an unconstrained string.

findings.title: Indexed access is typed Book but is Book | undefined at runtime; the author's own guard is dead code per the types
findings.description:
`tsconfig.json` sets `strict: true` but not `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, so `targetPool[Math.floor(...)]` at line 70 is typed `Book` when the runtime value is `Book | undefined`. The type is lying — narrowly, but demonstrably.

NO LIVE DEFECT: `targetPool` is provably non-empty here (line 59 returns early on `books.length === 0`, and line 69 falls back to `books` when the Finished filter is empty), and line 71 guards defensively anyway. Reported because it is the clearest concrete instance in this lot of the flag gap the audit should document: the author wrote a runtime guard that the compiler considers unreachable (`!randomBook` is 'always false' under the current type), which is precisely the signal that the declared type does not match reality. If the guard were ever removed as apparent dead code, line 73-74 would pass `undefined` to `setDailyBook` and `randomBook.id` would throw.

Enabling `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` would make the type honest and the guard mandatory. Be honest about cost: it is a repo-wide flag whose blast radius extends well past this lot — scope it as a project decision, not a local fix. Anchored here as a representative instance; the flag itself belongs to whichever lot owns tsconfig.json.

findings.title: Route paths and param names are bare strings with no compile-time link to their navigation consumers
findings.description:
Every route path in `routeTable` is an unbranded `string` literal, and every navigation target elsewhere is an independently-written `string`. Nothing connects producer to consumer, so renaming a route is invisible to the compiler.

CONCRETE FAILURE PAIRS:
- `path: 'review'` (line 21) vs `to: '/review'` in `NAV_ITEMS` (src/app/AppShell.tsx:20). Rename either and the nav link compiles fine, then 404s into the ErrorBoundary — which per L08-F02 shows a generic 'Something went wrong' rather than anything diagnostic.
- `path: 'profile'` (line 23) vs `to: '/profile'` (AppShell.tsx:22). Same.
- `path: 'book/:id'` (line 19) vs the template literals `navigate(`/book/${created.id}`)` (AppShell.tsx:194) and `navigate(`/book/${dailyBook.id}`)` (AppShell.tsx:213).
- The param name `:id` (lines 19-20) vs `useParams<{ id: string }>()` (src/features/book/useBookRoute.ts:8). Renaming `:id` to `:bookId` compiles; `id` then comes back `undefined`, `books.find(c => c.id === undefined)` matches nothing, and useBookRoute.ts:18 redirects the user home. A silent bounce to the library instead of a compile error.

Test coverage does not backstop this: src/app/routing.test.tsx exercises `/`, `/book/:id` and `/stats`, but never `/review` or `/profile`, so a rename of either would ship.

Severity is deliberately LOW — this is the well-known ergonomic gap in react-router's untyped mode, not a defect in the code, and the consumer side (useBookRoute) handles the missing param correctly. Fix shape: react-router 8 ships `href()` plus route typegen for exactly this; short of that, a shared `ROUTES` const object with `as const` paths gives producer/consumer a single source of truth.

findings.title: Unchecked-indexed-access cluster: 7 sites across the lot typed `string` where the runtime can yield `undefined`
findings.description: CLUSTER, reported once rather than seven times because the cause is a single tsconfig flag. With `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` off, every array/regex index in these three files is typed as if it always hits. Sites: BookDetail.tsx:71 `headerMatch[1].length` and 72 `headerMatch[2]`; EReader.tsx:71 `(trimmed.match(/^#+/) || [''])[0].length`, 130 `const [num, ...rest] = trimmed.split('.')`, 141 `trimmed.charAt(0)`; ProfileView.tsx:80 `.map((n) => n[0])`. Every one of these is currently SAFE by construction - the regex groups are non-optional and guarded by a preceding `startsWith` test, `split` always returns at least one element, and `Array.prototype.join` stringifies `undefined` to `''` so `getInitials('')` yields `''` rather than throwing. They are listed as the migration cost of turning the flag on, not as live bugs. The one site in this lot that is a live bug is EReader.tsx:395 (L11-F07), which the same flag would have caught at the keystroke. FIX SHAPE: enable `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, fix EReader.tsx:395 properly, and satisfy these six with non-null-safe narrowing (`?? ''`, destructuring defaults) rather than `!`. Effort is small in this lot but the flag is repo-wide, so cost must be measured across all of `src` before enabling.

findings.title: Blob MIME type is a bare `string` carried from storage into `window.open` with no check
findings.description: `StoredBlob.type` is declared `string` (types.ts:79) and is whatever `blob.type` happened to be at upload (repo.ts:138). `blobs.get` reconstructs `new Blob([record.bytes], { type: record.type })` (repo.ts:144) - so the returned `Blob` carries an unvalidated MIME string that the type system says nothing about. BookDetail line 197-200 asks for the `'pdf'` blob and hands the resulting object URL to `window.open`. If the stored `type` is `''` (which happens for any `File` the browser could not sniff) or anything other than `application/pdf`, the browser does not render the PDF in a tab - it downloads it or opens a blank tab, and the 'Open Original PDF' button appears broken with no error. The `BlobKind` discriminator (`'pdf' | 'audio-short' | 'audio-long'`) is a proper literal union and IS correctly used at the call site, but it is not connected to the MIME string, so the two can disagree freely. VERIFIED NEGATIVE on the null path: `blobs.get` honestly returns `Blob | undefined` and line 198 handles it with an early return - no cast, no `!`. FIX SHAPE: type the MIME as a small literal union (or brand it) keyed off `BlobKind`, and set it from the kind rather than trusting the uploaded file's sniffed type. Separately worth noting (not a type finding): the object URLs created on lines 160 and 199 are never revoked, so each audio generation and each PDF open leaks a blob for the lifetime of the document.

findings.title: `coverImageUrl: string` doubles as a "no cover" sentinel that only BookCard knows about; DailyWisdomModal renders it raw
findings.description: `Book.coverImageUrl` is typed `string` but carries out-of-band sentinel values for "no cover": the empty string, produced by the legacy migration (`legacy.coverImageUrl ?? ''`, migrate.ts:114), and — per BookCard's defensive check — the literal text `'null'`. BookCard is the only consumer that knows this: it substitutes a generated placeholder for both and installs an `onError` handler (BookCard.tsx:17-23, 57). DailyWisdomModal renders the value straight into `` with neither guard, so a migrated book with an empty cover produces ``, which browsers resolve to the current document URL — a request for the SPA's own HTML, decoded as an image, yielding a broken-image glyph inside the daily-wisdom card. BookDetail.tsx:241 has the same raw usage. The type is doing double duty (a URL *or* one of two absence markers) with no discriminator, which is why the knowledge of the sentinels lives in one component's `if` instead of in the type. Fix shape: make absence explicit — `coverImageUrl?: string` with a single shared `coverSrc(book)` helper that applies `placeholderCover` — so no consumer can forget. Blast radius: 3 render sites, 1 of which handles it.

findings.title: `monthlyGoal: number` permits 0 and NaN, producing `strokeDasharray="NaN, 100"`
findings.description: `Profile.monthlyGoal` is a bare `number` (types.ts:21) where the domain is 'a positive integer'. Line 53 divides by it unguarded: `Math.min(100, (finishedCount / profile.monthlyGoal) * 100)`. A `monthlyGoal` of 0 makes the expression `Infinity` when any book is finished and `NaN` when none are, and line 209 then emits `strokeDasharray={`${NaN}, 100`}` - an invalid SVG attribute that the browser rejects with a console error and a mis-rendered progress ring. The write side is equally unbranded: line 239 stores `parseInt(e.target.value)`, whose TypeScript type is `number` but whose runtime range includes `NaN`. Reachability is low today - `profiles.create` defaults to 4 (repo.ts:21) and the range input is `min="1"` - but nothing prevents a 0 or a NaN arriving from the unvalidated backup import (L11-F04) or a migrated legacy record, and once written it is durable. FIX SHAPE: brand it as a positive integer validated at the repo boundary, or at minimum guard the division with a sensible floor at the read site.

findings.title: `Record<string, number>` claims total key coverage; only a `|| 0` coercion saves the read of a key that does not exist yet
findings.description: `Record<string, number>` asserts that *every* string key yields a `number`. With `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` off, `categoryMap[b.category]` on line 25 is typed `number` while returning `undefined` on the first occurrence of each category — `undefined + 1` would be `NaN`, and the only thing preventing a row of "NaN book(s)" in the Category Breakdown is the `|| 0` fallback. The code is correct today; the *type* is not, and the correctness depends on a coercion the compiler cannot see. This is the clearest small illustration of what enabling `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` would buy: it would type this access `number | undefined` and force the fallback to be visible in the type, and it would simultaneously flag the genuinely dangerous accesses (L12-F04's `options[correctAnswerIndex]`, L12-F13's `items[0]!`). Cost is not a switch flip — every array index and `Record` read in the repo would need review — but the repo is small and already clean under `strict: true`, so it is achievable. Fix shape: either `Map<string, number>` (whose `get` honestly returns `| undefined`) or enable the flag.

findings.title: DialogProps.size is a raw string interpolated into className, and no test ever passes a non-default value
findings.description: DialogProps declares `size?: string` (Dialog.tsx:11-12) for what is really a closed set of Tailwind max-width classes, and Dialog.tsx:35 interpolates it directly into the panel's className. Every render in this suite (lines 11, 64, 88) omits `size`, so the only value ever exercised is the 'max-w-xl' default. Two production callers pass real values that no test covers: ApiKeyDialog.tsx:38 (`size="max-w-lg"`) and ConfirmDialog.tsx:43 (`size="max-w-md"`). Because the parameter is a bare string, a typo ('max-w-x1'), a class Tailwind will purge, or an unrelated utility class all compile and silently render a full-width panel with no visual regression signal. Fix shape: narrow to a union of the permitted classes (or a semantic 'sm' | 'md' | 'lg' mapped internally), which turns every typo into a compile error and makes the closed set self-documenting.

findings.title: `Dialog`'s `size` prop is a bare `string` where only a handful of Tailwind max-width classes are valid
findings.description: `size?: string` accepts any string, but the only values that do anything are Tailwind max-width utilities — and Tailwind's JIT compiler only emits classes it finds in the source, so a typo (`max-w-mdd`), a runtime-computed value, or a plausible-looking alternative (`w-96`) compiles cleanly, passes lint, and produces a dialog with no width constraint at all: the panel stretches to the full flex container. Nothing fails; the layout is just silently wrong, and only on the one screen that used the bad value. The existing call sites pass `"max-w-md"` (ConfirmDialog.tsx:42) and `"max-w-lg"` (ApiKeyDialog.tsx:38) with the `"max-w-xl"` default (line 15), so a three-member literal union — or a `'sm' | 'md' | 'lg'` token mapped to classes inside Dialog — would cover every use and make the invalid states unrepresentable. Fix shape: replace `string` with a literal union; trivial effort, 3 call sites.

findings.title: Redundant non-null assertions on array indices mark a tsconfig gap the tests would then mask
findings.description: `const [a, b] = getToasts(); expect(a!.id).not.toBe(b!.id)` (lines 24-25) and `dismissToast(getToasts()[0]!.id)` (line 30) apply `!` to values the compiler already types as non-optional: noUncheckedIndexedAccess is off, so `getToasts()[0]` and a destructured element both infer as ToastMessage. The assertions are therefore no-ops that the type system does not need -- they signal the authors expected the flag to be on. The finding is forward-looking: these `!`s are pre-installed suppressions. If noUncheckedIndexedAccess is ever enabled (a change that would correctly surface the real lying-index type at useReviewQueue.ts:46, see L14-F07), this file and the same pattern at reviewQueue.test.tsx:95/112 will keep compiling silently instead of flagging that the tests assume a non-empty array. Fix shape: drop the redundant `!` now, or assert length first, so that enabling the flag produces an honest signal. Separately, the suite covers only the 'error' and 'success' arms of ToastKind; the 'info' arm is safe only because Toast.tsx:8 uses `Record<ToastKind, ...>`, which the compiler checks exhaustively.

findings.title: The subscribe/emit store shape is hand-rolled twice, byte-identically, in `toastStore.ts` and `lib/ai/apiKey.ts`
findings.description: Both modules implement the same `useSyncExternalStore` backing store with the same three declarations copy-pasted: `const listeners = new Set<() => void>()`, an `emit()` that iterates it, and a `subscribeTo*(listener: () => void): () => void` that adds and returns a remover. The types are correct in both (no `Function`, no `unknown` payload, no untyped listener — see the verified negatives), so this is a duplication finding, not a soundness one: two sources of truth for one contract, and any future change (e.g. adding an unsubscribe-idempotency guard or a snapshot-version counter for `useSyncExternalStore` tearing) has to be made in two places or they drift. A single `createStore<T>()` returning `{ getSnapshot, subscribe, emit }` collapses both and makes the snapshot type a parameter rather than a per-module convention. Effort is trivial and the risk is low because both call sites already consume it through `useSyncExternalStore`. Blast radius: 2 modules, 2 React consumers (Toast.tsx:19 and the API-key hook).

findings.title: `document.activeElement as HTMLElement | null` asserts a `.focus()` method onto a base `Element`
findings.description: `document.activeElement` is `Element | null`. `Element` has no `focus()` — the cast is what makes `restoreTo?.focus()` on line 29 compile, and the `?.` guards only nullness, not the method's existence. In practice most focusable nodes are `HTMLElement` or `SVGElement` (both of which implement `focus()`), so this is Low rather than a live crash; the concrete risk is that the assertion is the only thing standing between the cleanup path and a `restoreTo.focus is not a function` TypeError thrown from an effect teardown — i.e. during unmount, where React surfaces it as an app-level error rather than a dismissible one. Fix shape: narrow with `instanceof HTMLElement` (or feature-test `'focus' in el`) instead of asserting; that also documents the intent. Same blast radius as L12-F07 (every modal in the app).

findings.title: Two non-null assertions on array indexing that are no-ops today and would become the only unguarded spots if `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` were enabled
findings.description: `items` is `HTMLElement[]` from `Array.from`, and with `noUncheckedIndexedAccess: false` (tsconfig.json has `strict: true` but not this flag) `items[0]` is already typed `HTMLElement` — so both `!` are currently no-ops that the compiler ignores. They are still worth recording for two reasons. First, they are inconsistent with line 26 of the same file, which handles the identical "first focusable element" access with `?.` instead — two idioms for one question in twelve lines. Second, they are pre-emptive: if the project later enables `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` (the single highest-value remaining strictness flag for this codebase — L12-F04's out-of-bounds quiz index and L12-F14's Record access are both instances of what it catches), these two lines will keep compiling silently while every other array access in the repo is forced to prove itself. The guard on line 45 does make them true today, so this is Low with no runtime failure. Fix shape: destructure with a length check, or use `at(0)`/`at(-1)` and handle `undefined`, so no assertion is needed either before or after the flag flips.

findings.title: The 'All' sentinel shares a value space with real, AI-generated category strings
findings.description: `activeCategory` is a bare `string` whose sentinel value 'All' lives in the same value space as real `book.category` values, and `Book.category` is itself untyped (`category: string`, src/types.ts:33) and populated from unconstrained model output: src/lib/ai/summarize.ts:26 `category: data.category || 'Other'`, whose response schema declares only `{ type: Type.STRING }` (src/lib/ai/schemas.ts:8) -- the eight-value constraint exists solely as English in the prompt (src/lib/ai/prompts.ts:12), and the `Category` enum in types.ts:6 is never bound to the field. So the set is NOT closed by the buttons: `categories` on line 65 is derived from stored data. If the model ever returns 'All' for a book, `categories` contains 'All' twice, `key={cat}` on line 173 collides, and the second button -- which looks like a category filter -- short-circuits the check on line 47 and shows every book instead of that category's. The same collision silently makes `showRecommendations` (line 110) true when a real category is selected. The file already demonstrates the correct pattern one line below: `statusFilter` is typed `'All' | BookStatus` (line 23). Fix shape: type the sentinel out of the data space -- `null` for 'no filter', or a tagged `{ kind: 'all' } | { kind: 'category'; name: string }` -- and narrow `Book.category` to the `Category` enum. Blast radius: this page's filter row.

findings.title: Priority score map typed `Record<string, number>` instead of `Record<Priority, number>`
findings.description: The key domain is `Priority` ('Low' | 'Medium' | 'High', src/types.ts:2), not `string`. Typing the map with a `string` index signature has two costs. First, the map stops being exhaustive: adding a fourth `Priority` value compiles cleanly and silently scores it 1, changing the 'Want to Read' ordering with no compile error anywhere. Second, the index access is a small lie in both directions -- with `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` off (confirmed in tsconfig.json) `priorityScore[...]` is typed `number` and never `undefined`, so the `?? 1` fallbacks on lines 57-58 are unreachable as far as the compiler is concerned while reading as though they were load-bearing; they are in fact dead, because `a.priority || 'Low'` can only produce a key that exists. `Record<Priority, number>` makes the literal exhaustive, makes the lookup genuinely total, and lets both `?? 1` fallbacks be deleted. Blast radius: the sort comparator on this page.

findings.title: A recommendation title doubles as its identity for both the React key and the in-flight marker
findings.description: `addingBookTitle: string | null` is a raw title used as an identity: it is compared against `rec.title` on lines 109 and 149 to decide which card shows the 'Generating...' spinner, and `rec.title` is also the React reconciliation key on line 81. Nothing guarantees titles are unique -- `Recommendation[]` comes from `getAIRecommendations` (src/lib/ai/recommend.ts:34), which maps model output straight through with no dedupe, and the defaults in recommendationDefaults.ts are a separate list that a refreshed set can overlap. Concrete failure: the model returns two entries with the same title (a common case for reissues, or a title the model repeats), so the list renders duplicate React keys and, once the user clicks one, BOTH cards show the 'Generating...' spinner while only one summary is being fetched -- and clicking the other is silently swallowed by the `if (addingBookTitle) return;` guard at LibraryPage.tsx:87. A distinct identity on `Recommendation` (or an index-based key plus an index-based in-flight marker) removes the ambiguity; a branded `RecommendationId` would make the title/identity mixup a compile error. Blast radius: the carousel and LibraryPage's preview flow.
