findings.title: The 'no active profile' precondition is unrepresentable in the mutators' return types, and is reported to the user as success
findings.description: Three sibling mutators handle the same precondition three different ways, and two of them encode failure as a legitimate-looking result. `importGoodreadsRows` returns `{ added: 0, duplicates: 0 }` for 'no profile' -- byte-identical to 'the file parsed but every row was already in the library' -- and GoodreadsImport.tsx:39-43 renders that as a green `toast.success('Imported 0 books.')`. `importLibrary` (line 104) returns `0` for the same state, which ProfileView.tsx:133 reports as 'Imported 0 new books.' Meanwhile `addBook` (line 42) throws `new Error('No active profile')` for the identical precondition. Honest reachability: App.tsx:22 does not mount `LibraryProvider` until `profile` is non-null, so these branches are dead in the current app -- the finding is that the return types cannot express the precondition, so nothing catches a future change to where the provider mounts, or a direct call from a test or a new caller, and the failure mode when it lands is a silent success message over dropped data. Fix shape: either make the precondition a type-level invariant (take the profile as an argument, so a null profile cannot reach the call) or return a tagged result so 'no profile' is a distinct case callers must handle. Blast radius: two call sites today, both user-facing toasts.

findings.title: The theme union is re-declared inline instead of importing ThemeChoice
findings.description: renderWithTheme's parameter re-states the literal union `'system' | 'light' | 'dark'` rather than importing ThemeChoice (useTheme.ts:5), which is itself `Profile['theme']` (types.ts:23). Three copies of the same union now exist. If a fourth theme is added to Profile, this helper keeps compiling (the narrower literal union is still assignable to what profiles.create accepts, repo.ts:16), the new value is silently untested, and nothing flags the divergence. The same duplication pattern would apply to any future test helper that re-types a domain union. Fix shape: `import type { ThemeChoice } from './useTheme'` and annotate the parameter with it, so adding a theme forces the helper (and any exhaustive switch on it) to be revisited.

findings.title: An unvalidated Profile.theme from IndexedDB is annotated into a three-literal union it may not belong to
findings.description:
`const theme: ThemeChoice = profile?.theme ?? 'system'` is the point where an unvalidated persisted value acquires a narrow type. `Profile` records come from `repo.profiles.list()`, which re-types raw IndexedDB rows without any runtime check, so `profile.theme` is `unknown` in practice. The `??` handles only null/undefined; a value like `"Dark"`, `"sepia"` or `"null"` passes straight through, and the explicit `ThemeChoice` annotation certifies to the compiler that it is one of `'system' | 'light' | 'dark'`. Line 27 then inherits the lie: the ternary's else-branch is believed to be `'light' | 'dark'` and is annotated `ResolvedTheme`, so `resolved` is typed as a two-literal union while holding an arbitrary string.

Concrete outcome (silent, not a crash): `classList.toggle('dark', resolved === 'dark')` at line 30 evaluates false, so the app renders in light mode with no error and no way for the user to tell why. In `ThemeToggle.tsx:24-26` the `theme === value` comparison is false for all three buttons, so `aria-pressed` is false on every one — the control group shows nothing selected, and a screen-reader user gets no current-state announcement. Clicking any button repairs it, so it self-heals on interaction.

Honest severity note: I traced every in-app writer and none can produce an out-of-union value. `repo.profiles.create` defaults `theme: input.theme ?? 'system'` (repo.ts:23); `useTheme.setTheme` only writes a `ThemeChoice`; `migrate.ts`'s `LegacyProfile` has no `theme` field at all, so migrated profiles get the default. The realistic vectors are a hand-edited IndexedDB record, a shared/downgraded browser profile, or a future theme value ('sepia' is a plausible addition given EReader owns its own reader themes) written by a newer build and read by an older one. Hence Low. The fix is a small parse-at-the-boundary guard rather than an annotation. Blast radius: `useTheme` is called at the shell level (`AppShell.tsx:31`) so it governs the whole app's dark mode.

findings.title: StatsPage destructures books without isLoading, so an unloaded library is typed identically to an empty one
findings.description:
`useLibrary()` returns `books: Book[]` alongside a separate `isLoading: boolean`, and `StatsPage` takes only `books`. `Book[]` cannot express 'not loaded yet', so the empty array returned before `reload()` resolves is indistinguishable — to the compiler and to the component — from a genuinely empty library. The type offers no prompt to check `isLoading`, and unlike `BookDetailPage.tsx:19` and `ReaderPage.tsx:14` (which do gate on `isLoading`), this page does not.

Concrete outcome: on navigation to /stats the user briefly sees a fully-rendered, confidently-wrong dashboard — 'Finished 0 out of 0', 'Total Learning 0m', 'Avg. Rating 0', 'No category data available yet', and the Wisdom Milestone copy reading 'enough knowledge to discuss deep concepts for over 0 hours straight' — which then flips to real numbers once IndexedDB responds. It reads as data loss for the instant it is on screen.

Verified negatives worth recording, because they were plausible and are not true: `StatsView` is arithmetic-safe on an empty array. Both `reduce` calls pass an initial value of 0 (StatsView.tsx:17, 20) so neither throws `TypeError` on an empty array; `avgRating` is guarded by `finished.length > 0` (line 19) so there is no NaN; and the only division by `stats.total` (line 153) sits inside a map over `categoryData`, which is empty whenever `total` is 0, so it never evaluates. No NaN and no throw — the defect is purely the untagged loading state.

Correct behavior: gate on `isLoading` here as the book pages do, or model the library state as a tagged union so the compiler forces the distinction. Blast radius: this page only; the underlying untagged loading bag in `useLibrary` is the shared root cause.

findings.title: AiError.kind carries the full union on every instance, so MissingKeyError does not narrow its own tag and per-kind payloads have nowhere to live
findings.description: `AiErrorKind` is a well-formed string-literal union and `kind` is the natural discriminant, but it is declared as the whole union on the base class, so no subclass refines it: `new MissingKeyError().kind` types as the full eight-member `AiErrorKind` even though it is unconditionally `'missing-key'`. The immediate cost is small and honest to state — `src/app/AppShell.tsx:49` (`aiError.kind === 'missing-key' || aiError.kind === 'invalid-key'`) is the only consumer that branches on the tag, and TypeScript would still flag a renamed member there as a no-overlap comparison, so the tag is not currently unsafe. The structural cost is that the union cannot carry per-kind data: `rate-limited` has a `retryDelay` in Google's RetryInfo detail and `invalid-key` has an HTTP status, but `AiError` can only stash them in `cause: unknown` (line 15), which no consumer in the repo reads. That is what forces the fix for L04-F01 to go through re-parsing rather than through the type. Correct shape: make `kind` a type parameter or declare `readonly kind: 'missing-key'` on `MissingKeyError`, and if per-kind data is ever needed, model `AiError` as a discriminated union over `kind` with a payload per member rather than a single class with an untyped `cause`. Blast radius: 1 branching consumer (AppShell.tsx:49), 1 subclass (MissingKeyError, constructed at client.ts:11), 2 test files.

findings.title: Redundant `bytes[i] as number` pre-suppresses exactly the check noUncheckedIndexedAccess would add
findings.description:
Under the current `tsconfig.json` (strict: true, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` NOT set), indexing a `Uint8Array` already yields `number` via its numeric index signature, so `as number` is a no-op assertion that the compiler does not need. It is not currently hiding a bug — the loop bound `i < bytes.length` makes every index provably in range.

It matters for a specific forward-looking reason that is squarely this audit's concern: if `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is enabled (a likely structural recommendation for this repo, since it is otherwise clean under strict), this cast is precisely the construct that would make the new flag a silent no-op at this site instead of surfacing the indexed-access question. A cast that exists only to pre-empt a strictness flag is indistinguishable from one that is masking a real out-of-bounds read, and a reviewer cannot tell them apart without re-deriving the loop bound.

Correct fix shape: delete the assertion (it is unnecessary today), and if `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is later enabled, restructure the loop with `for (const byte of bytes)` so the element type is `number` without any assertion.

Blast radius: one line, internal to this module. `bytesToBase64` itself has no production caller — grep shows it is imported only by `src/lib/base64.test.ts`.

findings.title: Truthy check on a numeric cover id conflates absent with zero
findings.description:
`coverId` is `number | undefined` and L8 tests it with a bare truthy check, so a cover id of `0` is treated identically to a missing one. This is the textbook `0`-is-falsy coercion bug: the intent is unmistakably 'did we get an id?', but the expression asks 'is the id non-zero?'. CORRECT BEHAVIOR: `typeof coverId === 'number'` (which also happens to close the L06-F02 validation hole in the same edit) or at minimum `coverId !== undefined`.

CONCRETE FAILURE: a record whose `cover_i` is `0` returns `null`, `fetchCover` falls through to `placeholderCover`, and the user gets a generated initials tile instead of the real cover. No crash and no data corruption — the failure is a silently-degraded image, which is why this is low.

NOTE ON THE SAME LINE IN THE SAME FUNCTION: the identical pattern appears at src/lib/covers/googleBooks.ts:24 (`if (url) return ...`), where the truthy check is on a `string` and correctly rejects `''`. That one is fine; only the numeric case is wrong.

findings.title: downloadText takes three adjacent bare-string positional params, so swapping filename and contents compiles cleanly
findings.description:
`downloadText(filename: string, contents: string, mimeType = 'text/markdown')` has three same-typed positional parameters where order is entirely load-bearing and the compiler cannot distinguish them. `downloadText(markdown, filename)` type-checks and silently produces a download whose filename is the entire markdown body (browsers truncate/sanitise it) containing the filename as its content. This is the classic branded-type foot-gun from the audit spec's red-team list.

The risk is live because both call sites build the two arguments inline in the same expression and could easily be transposed during a refactor: `src/components/ProfileView.tsx:92` — `downloadText(\`booksum-library-${new Date().toISOString().split('T')[0]}.md\`, markdown)` — and `src/components/BookDetail.tsx:417` — `downloadText(\`${slugify(book.title)}.md\`, bookToMarkdown(book, summary))`.

`mimeType` is likewise a bare `string` interpolated into a Content-Type at line 3 (`\`${mimeType};charset=utf-8\``); passing an already-parameterised value such as `'text/csv;charset=iso-8859-1'` would emit a double `charset` with no type error. No current call site does.

Correct behaviour: take a single options object (`{ filename, contents, mimeType }`), or brand `Filename` / `MimeType`. An options object is the cheaper fix here and removes the ordering hazard entirely.

VERIFIED NEGATIVES for this file: `document.createElement('a')` is correctly used without a cast (it already returns `HTMLAnchorElement`), there are no element or DOM type assertions anywhere in the file, and `URL.revokeObjectURL(url)` IS called (line 11), so there is no object-URL leak. `slugify`'s `|| 'untitled'` at line 21 is a truthy check on a string where the empty-string branch is the intended behaviour, not a coercion bug.

Blast radius: 2 call sites.

findings.title: `columnOf` returns a bare `number` hiding a `-1` not-found sentinel that no type can narrow
findings.description:
`columnOf` (L83) has no return annotation and infers `number` from `Array.prototype.indexOf`, so the `-1` not-found sentinel is completely invisible in the type. All six derived constants (L85-90 `titleAt`, `authorAt`, `ratingAt`, `shelfAt`, `isbnAt`, `dateReadAt`) are typed `number`, and 'column 3' and 'column not present' are indistinguishable to the compiler. CORRECT BEHAVIOR: return `number | null` (or a small `{found: true, index} | {found: false}` union) so consumers must narrow before indexing.

CONCRETE FAILURE 1 (footgun, latent): index `0` is a valid column AND is falsy. The current `cell()` helper checks `index >= 0` correctly, but any future refactor to the idiomatic-looking `if (titleAt)` silently drops the column-0 case — which the repo's own test at src/lib/goodreads.test.ts:67 exercises (`'Title,Author,Exclusive Shelf\nDune,Herbert,read'`, Title at index 0). The type gives no hint that `0` is meaningful.

CONCRETE FAILURE 2 (live, user-visible): when the `title` header is absent entirely — a non-Goodreads CSV, or an export with localised/renamed headers — `titleAt` is `-1`, `cell(-1)` returns `''` for every row, so every row hits the `if (!title)` branch at L99 and increments `skipped`. The user sees '0 books found' (GoodreadsImport.tsx:27-29) plus 'N rows skipped' with no indication that the problem is a missing header rather than an empty file. A narrowable return type would force this case to be handled explicitly at the top of the function.

BLAST RADIUS: 6 call sites inside this file; no external consumers.

findings.title: `dateRead` is parsed and typed as `string` with no format contract, then silently discarded
findings.description:
`GoodreadsRow.dateRead?: string` (L9) is populated at L113 from raw file content with zero validation — no format check, no parse, no `isNaN(d.getTime())` guard. Two distinct problems.

PROBLEM 1 (live, and the reason this is only low): the field has NO consumer. `importGoodreadsRows` (src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:150-160) maps `title`, `author`, `status`, `rating` and `isbn13` but never reads `dateRead`, so `Book.finishedAt` is left `undefined` for every imported book — including books imported as `'Finished'`. A repo-wide grep confirms `finishedAt` is declared at src/types.ts:40 and written NOWHERE in `src/`. The exported type therefore advertises data the pipeline discards, which is a type-honesty defect: a consumer reading `GoodreadsParseResult` reasonably concludes read-dates survive the import. They do not.

PROBLEM 2 (latent, and the brief's `Invalid Date` hypothesis): because nothing consumes it, there is currently NO `new Date(csvString)` anywhere in this lot — VERIFIED NEGATIVE. But the moment someone wires it up, Goodreads writes this column as `YYYY/MM/DD`, which is NOT an ISO-8601 form and is parsed inconsistently across engines; `new Date('2023/05/14')` is engine- and locale-dependent, and a blank or malformed cell yields `Invalid Date` — which is STILL typed `Date`, propagating a silently-broken value into `Book.finishedAt` and any date arithmetic downstream. The repo contains no `isNaN(getTime())` validation anywhere to catch it.

CORRECT BEHAVIOR: either drop the field from `GoodreadsRow` (it is dead weight that misleads), or validate it into an ISO date string at the parse boundary and actually map it to `Book.finishedAt`.

findings.title: `isbn13` is an unvalidated bare `string` interpolated unencoded into a persisted cover URL
findings.description: `cleanIsbn` (L69-72) strips Goodreads' `="..."` spreadsheet armour and returns whatever is left, typed as `isbn13?: string` (L8). Nothing checks it is 13 characters, or digits, or an ISBN at all — the name is the only thing asserting the domain. `coverForIsbn` (L121) then takes a bare `string | undefined` and interpolates it into a URL WITHOUT `encodeURIComponent`. CORRECT BEHAVIOR: a branded `Isbn13` type produced by a validating parser (`/^\d{13}$/`), plus `encodeURIComponent` at the interpolation site. CONCRETE FAILURE 1 (type mix-up — the classic branded-type footgun): `coverForIsbn(isbn13: string | undefined)` accepts ANY string, so `coverForIsbn(row.title)` type-checks perfectly and produces a garbage URL. Same-typed primitives with distinct domains are exactly what branding prevents. CONCRETE FAILURE 2 (live data quality): a 10-digit ISBN, an ASIN, or an ISSN passes through untouched and yields a 404 cover; an ISBN cell containing a space, `#`, `?`, or `/` (hand-edited CSV, or a mis-detected column) produces a malformed URL. That URL is PERSISTED to `Book.coverImageUrl` in IndexedDB at src/features/library/useLibrary.tsx:158 and later rendered as an ``, so the bad value outlives the import session and is only masked by BookCard's `onError` placeholder swap (src/components/BookCard.tsx:18/27). SECURITY BOUNDING (checked, deliberately not overclaimed): the value is interpolated after a fixed `https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/isbn/` path prefix, so it cannot change origin, and it lands in an `img src` rather than a script context — this is a data-quality and URL-correctness issue, not an SSRF or XSS one. VERIFIED CORRECT: the `/^="?|"?$/g` regex does handle Goodreads' real formats — `="9780735211292"` -> `9780735211292`, `=""` -> `''` -> `undefined` (matching the test at src/lib/goodreads.test.ts:27), and a bare ISBN passes through unchanged.

findings.title: Summary.model is a bare string, so nothing type-checks that a persisted model id is a real one
findings.description: `model: string` records which Gemini model produced a summary, with `'legacy'` as a documented sentinel for migrated rows. `src/lib/ai/models.ts` already declares `MODELS` with `as const`, so the exact union `(typeof MODELS)[keyof typeof MODELS] | 'legacy'` is available at zero cost. As typed, any string is accepted: a typo'd or hand-edited model id round-trips through the store unnoticed, and — relevant to the project's stated invariant that model IDs live only in `src/lib/ai/models.ts` — nothing stops a literal model id being written from elsewhere, which is exactly what `src/lib/storage/migrate.ts:131` does with `model: 'legacy'`. Impact is low today because the field is currently only recorded, not dispatched on; it becomes a real problem the moment any code branches on it or a model is renamed and stale ids need finding. Correct shape: narrow the field to the union derived from `MODELS` plus the `'legacy'` sentinel, which makes a Google model rename a compile error at every stale write site rather than a silent data inconsistency.

findings.title: The quiz-question shape is declared three separate times across types.ts and srs.ts
findings.description: `QuizQuestion` (types.ts:105-110) declares `question`, `options`, `correctAnswerIndex`, `explanation`. `ReviewCard` (types.ts:86-89) re-declares the identical four fields inline alongside its id and SRS fields. `NewCardInput` (src/lib/srs.ts:13-20) declares them a third time alongside `profileId`/`bookId`, and `src/lib/srs.ts:26-30` then copies them across field-by-field. One shape, three declarations, one hand-written copy loop. Adding or renaming a quiz field means editing three types and the copy loop, and the compiler only flags a subset of those — a field added to `QuizQuestion` alone silently fails to reach `ReviewCard`, which is how quiz data would quietly stop being persisted. Correct shape: define the four fields once and compose — `interface ReviewCard extends QuizQuestion { id; profileId; bookId; ease; intervalDays; dueAt; reviewCount }` and `type NewCardInput = QuizQuestion & { profileId: string; bookId: string }` — which also collapses the copy loop in `newCard` to a spread.

findings.title: noImplicitOverride is off — one unmarked override in the AI error class hierarchy
findings.description:
`noImplicitOverride` is not enabled. Measured: `npx tsc --noEmit --noImplicitOverride` produces exactly 1 error, at `src/lib/ai/errors.ts:15`, where a constructor parameter property redeclares a member inherited from `Error` without an `override` modifier.

Without the flag, a subclass member that shadows a base-class member is indistinguishable from one that was meant to be new. On an `Error` subclass this is the classic footgun: silently redeclaring `message`, `name` or `cause` as a parameter property can shadow the base field that `Error.prototype.toString`, the `stack` header and most logging paths read from, so the error renders with an empty or stale message while the subclass field holds the real one. It also means a future rename in the base type would silently orphan the subclass member rather than erroring.

Correct behaviour: enable `noImplicitOverride` and add the explicit `override` keyword at that one site — or, if the redeclaration is not actually intended to override, drop the parameter property and pass the value through to `super()`. Adoption cost: trivial, one line, and it is the only blocker for turning the flag on permanently.

findings.title: Four zero-cost strictness flags are unset — they add 0 errors today but nothing locks the property in
findings.description:
Four checking flags outside the `strict` family are not enabled, and each measures **0 errors** against the current source, so enabling them is a pure ratchet with no remediation work at all:

- `noImplicitReturns` (0 errors) — would catch a function with a conditional return path that falls through to `undefined`.
- `noUncheckedSideEffectImports` (0 errors) — would catch `import './missing.css'`-style imports that resolve to nothing.
- `allowUnreachableCode: false` (0 errors) — currently unreachable code is a suggestion-level hint, not an error.
- `allowUnusedLabels: false` (0 errors).

Because `strict: true` already covers the whole strict family (verified below), these four plus the flags in L01-F02/F03/F05/F09 are the entire remaining strictness surface. The codebase is clean enough today that all four can be turned on in a single commit with no code changes; leaving them off means the first violation lands silently rather than failing CI.

For completeness, I verified that `strict: true` really does enable every sub-flag in TypeScript 6.0.3 — passing each explicitly adds 0 errors: `noImplicitAny`, `strictNullChecks`, `noImplicitThis`, `strictFunctionTypes`, `strictBindCallApply`, `strictPropertyInitialization`, `strictBuiltinIteratorReturn`, `useUnknownInCatchVariables`. So there is no hidden strict-family gap; the codebase is genuinely null-aware, and the multi-week `strictNullChecks` migration the audit spec warns about does not apply here.

findings.title: skipLibCheck: true masks an unresolved module in the @google/genai type surface (legitimate, but undocumented)
findings.description:
`skipLibCheck: true` is set. Measured what it hides: `npx tsc --noEmit --skipLibCheck false` produces exactly 2 errors, both in `node_modules`, none in source:

1. `node_modules/@google/genai/dist/genai.d.ts(1,29)` — cannot resolve `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js`. This is an **optional** peer dependency of `@google/genai` (`peerDependenciesMeta: { "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk": { optional: true } }`) and is deliberately not installed.
2. `node_modules/@testing-library/jest-dom/types/jest.d.ts(1,23)` — cannot find type definitions for `jest`, which this project correctly does not have (it uses Vitest).

So `skipLibCheck` is load-bearing, not laziness — this is the "compatibility lock-in" pattern the audit spec says to isolate rather than rip out, and the recommendation is NOT to turn it off. Blast radius today is nil: the unresolved `Client` type is only referenced by `@google/genai`'s MCP tool helper, and the app imports only `GoogleGenAI`, `Chat`, `Type` and `Modality` (`src/lib/ai/client.ts:1`, `chat.ts:1`, `schemas.ts:1`, `tts.ts:1`), none of which touch it.

The real gap is that this is undocumented. Every other non-obvious setting in this repo carries a comment explaining why (see `vite.config.ts:5-8` and `:13-15`, and `.github/workflows/ci.yml:15-16`), but `skipLibCheck` does not — so a future contributor cannot tell whether it is deliberate insulation or an unexamined default, and will not know that flipping it breaks the build for a reason unrelated to their change. Correct behaviour: add a comment naming both causes, and re-run `--skipLibCheck false` on dependency bumps so newly-introduced third-party type drift is noticed rather than permanently silenced.

findings.title: Vitest and jest-dom globals are in the type scope of production source, not just tests
findings.description:
`"types": ["vite/client", "vitest/globals", "@testing-library/jest-dom"]` applies to the whole program, and `node_modules/vitest/globals.d.ts` uses `declare global` to publish `describe`, `it`, `test`, `expect`, `vi`, `beforeEach`, `afterEach` and friends. Combined with `include: ["src", "vite.config.ts"]` — a single program covering all 86 source files, of which 21 are tests — this means a production module such as `src/lib/storage/repo.ts` or a React component can reference `vi.fn()` or `expect(...)` and `tsc --noEmit` will accept it. The failure only appears in the browser at runtime as `vi is not defined`, and it ships in the bundle.

ESLint does not backstop this either: `no-undef` is explicitly disabled for TypeScript files by the `tseslint` recommended preset (confirmed via `--print-config`: `no-undef: [0, {"typeof": false}]`), on the assumption that the compiler catches undefined identifiers — which here it does not, because the globals are genuinely declared.

Correct behaviour: split the program so test globals are scoped to test files — either a `tsconfig.test.json` covering `**/*.test.ts(x)` and `src/test/**` that adds `vitest/globals` and `@testing-library/jest-dom`, with the root config dropping them; or drop `globals: true` from `vite.config.ts:11` and import `describe`/`it`/`expect`/`vi` explicitly in tests. Adoption cost is moderate: the second option touches all 21 test files (mechanical, one import line each) and would require dropping `"vitest/globals"` from `types` in the same commit. Severity is Low because no production file currently does this — the finding is that nothing prevents it.

findings.title: `HTMLMediaElement.duration` enters state as a plain `number` that can be `NaN` or `Infinity`, and is then both formatted and truthiness-tested
findings.description: `duration` is media metadata decoded by the browser — external data crossing into typed code with no validation. `HTMLMediaElement.duration` is `NaN` when unknown and `Infinity` for streams or containers without a duration header, and `number` claims neither is possible. Two consequences downstream: `formatTime(duration)` (line 217) computes `Math.floor(Infinity / 60)` and `Infinity % 60`, rendering the literal string "Infinity:NaN" in the transport bar (and "NaN:NaN" for NaN); and `max={duration || 100}` (line 212) uses a truthiness test on a number, which cannot distinguish "duration is genuinely 0" from "duration is unknown" — both silently become a 100-second scrubber whose thumb position is meaningless. Severity is Low because the app's only audio source is a locally generated WAV blob, whose header carries a finite duration, so the bad values are not reachable on the current happy path. Fix shape: validate at the assignment — `Number.isFinite(d) ? d : 0` — and use an explicit `duration: number | null` so "unknown" is a state the renderer must handle rather than a magic falsy number. Adjacent observation, filed here only for context because rejection handling belongs to the error-recovery audit: `togglePlay` (line 50) discards the `Promise<void>` from `.play()`, and `setIsPlaying(!isPlaying)` on line 52 flips the UI optimistically — if `play()` rejects (autoplay policy, or an AbortError when `src` changes), neither a `play` nor a `pause` event fires, so the button shows Pause over silent audio until the user clicks twice.
